nodes.title: P·Bergmann (1974) — ★ ABM Root
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Bergmann, B. R. (1974). A microsimulation of the macroeconomy with explicitly represented money flows. *Annals of Economic and Social Measurement*, 3(3), 475–489.

---

## Intro

The **founding paper of agent-based macroeconomics.** In 1974 macro was dominated by representative-agent theory (Lucas 1972; Sargent-Wallace 1975) — one household, one firm, closed-form solutions. Bergmann rejected the aggregation and asked: *what if we simulate every actor explicitly, track every dollar between them, and let the macro emerge?* She built the first full-economy agent-based model, decades before "ABM" had a name.

## Methodology — how the agents are built

- **Firms.** State = inventory, price, workforce, cash. Each period they plan production from past sales, set prices as markup, pay wages, buy inputs, invest.
- **Households.** State = wage income, transfers, taxes, portfolio. They receive income, pay taxes, choose consumption/savings, allocate wealth.
- **Banks + central bank.** Buy/sell government bonds, set the interest rate.

Every action posts a **double-entry accounting** entry. Decision rules from **operations research** (safety stock, markup pricing), not from optimization. Twelve sequential steps per period.

## Results & Contribution

- First **full-economy micro-simulation.** Every dollar tracked from source to sink.
- **Stock-flow consistent** decades before Godley-Lavoie codified it.
- Predicted **stagflation** — the 1970s combination of high inflation + high unemployment that broke Phillips-curve theory.
- **Ancestor of every macro ABM below** — EURACE, K+S, CATS all inherit her 12-step architecture.

→ Anchor: **★ Incentives Theory Core**

nodes.title: P·Axtell (2001) — Endogenous Firms
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Axtell, R. (2001). *Effort dynamics in economic organizations.* Santa Fe Institute Working Paper 99-11-076. Extended in Axtell (2018).

---

## Intro

Firms are **not primitives** — they emerge endogenously from workers' effort and mobility choices.

## What it adds to Bergmann (1974)

Bergmann assumed firms exist. Axtell:
- **No exogenous firms** — a firm is defined as a set of workers who cooperate and share output equally (team pay, Kandel–Lazear 1992 style).
- Each period, each worker chooses effort AND membership (stay / leave / found / join).
- **Sisyphean cycle**: firms grow → free-rider gap widens → high-effort members leave → firm collapses → members disperse and form new smaller firms.

## Results

- **Zipf's law emerges** — the steady-state firm-size distribution matches US Census data (Simon–Bonini 1958 empirical fact finally has a bottom-up model).
- **Kandel–Lazear peer-pressure logic played out dynamically** — the analytical PA result on team-size dilution becomes a dynamic industrial pattern.

→ Anchor: **P·Bergmann (1974)**

nodes.title: P·EURACE (Dawid et al., 2008–2012)
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Dawid, H., Gemkow, S., Harting, P., van der Hoog, S. & Neugart, M. (2012). *The EURACE@Unibi Model: An Agent-Based Macroeconomic Model for Economic Policy Analysis.* Working paper, Bielefeld University. Continued in Dawid et al. (2018) and several *JEDC* articles.

---

## Intro

The **largest published macro ABM** — 50,000+ agents simulating a European economy. Built by the Bielefeld group under an EU-funded project.

## What it adds to Bergmann (1974)

Bergmann proved the concept at ~1,000 agents with operations-research rules. EURACE:
- **Scales 50×** to prove ABM computationally feasible against DSGE.
- **Uses management-science rules** (Basel-style bank capital, Taylor-rule central bank, markup pricing, inventory targets) — blunts the "arbitrary heuristics" critique because every rule is what real firms do.
- **Multi-market, stock-flow consistent** across labor / goods / credit / capital.

## Results

Reproduces macro stylised facts without any optimising agent: Beveridge curve, endogenous business cycles, wage–price spiral, financial-fragility clustering, distributional dynamics.

→ Anchor: **P·Bergmann (1974)**

nodes.title: P·Dosi–Fagiolo–Roventini (2010) — K+S
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Dosi, G., Fagiolo, G. & Roventini, A. (2010). Schumpeter meeting Keynes: A policy-friendly model of endogenous growth and business cycles. *Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control*, 34(9), 1748–1767.

---

## Intro

The **K+S ("Keynes + Schumpeter") model** — flagship of the Pisa–Sant'Anna evolutionary tradition.

## What it adds to Bergmann (1974)

Bergmann's model had no innovation dynamics. K+S adds:
- **Two-sector economy**: capital-good firms (Schumpeter — do R&D, innovate/imitate) + consumer-good firms (Keynes — demand-constrained production).
- **Endogenous productivity growth** from R&D + selection: winners grow, losers exit.
- **Growth and business cycles unified.** In booms, high demand → R&D up → productivity grows. In recessions, weak firms exit → productivity distribution improves. Cycles are the mechanism through which growth happens.

## Results

Reproduces joint growth + business-cycle stylised facts. Used for climate-policy simulations (Lamperti et al. 2018), inequality (Dosi et al. 2015), fiscal counterfactuals.

→ Anchor: **P·Bergmann (1974)**

nodes.title: P·Delli Gatti et al. (2011) — CATS
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Delli Gatti, D., Desiderio, S., Gaffeo, E., Cirillo, P. & Gallegati, M. (2011). *Macroeconomics from the Bottom-Up*. Springer.

---

## Intro

**CATS** — the Ancona/Politecnico-Milano group. Where K+S emphasises Schumpeterian innovation, CATS emphasises **credit-network fragility**: cascading firm bankruptcies as the endogenous source of macroeconomic crises. First rigorous ABM implementation of Minsky's (1986) financial-instability hypothesis.

## What it adds to Bergmann (1974)

Bergmann had banks but no network topology. CATS adds:
- **Firm–bank bipartite credit network** — every firm has a debt relationship with a specific bank.
- **Firm–firm supply-chain network** — cascading defaults through both networks.
- **Endogenous financial crises** without exogenous banking shocks.

## Results

- Recurrent fat-tailed recessions without imposed shocks.
- **Network topology first-order** — density and capital-ratio thresholds determine systemic-risk properties.
- Extended in Battiston et al. (2016, *Nature Communications*) to cross-country systemic risk.

→ Anchor: **P·Bergmann (1974)**

nodes.title: P·Fagiolo–Dosi–Gabriele (2004) — Evolutionary Labor
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Fagiolo, G., Dosi, G. & Gabriele, R. (2004). Matching, bargaining, and wage setting in an evolutionary model of labor and output markets. *International Journal of Modern Physics C*, 15, 1–16.

---

## Intro

First labor-market ABM where **wage-setting rules themselves evolve** via replicator dynamics — not just agent-level learning, population-level rule selection.

## What it adds to Bergmann (1974)

Bergmann had firms following fixed operations-research rules. FDG:
- **Search-matching labor market** with heterogeneous workers and firms.
- Each firm follows ONE wage-setting rule from a menu (markup over cost, follow the leader, efficiency wage, local adjustment).
- **Replicator dynamics on the rules**: high-profit rules spread; low-profit rules exit.

## Results

- Reproduces Beveridge curve, Okun's law, wage–productivity co-movement.
- **Explains institutional inertia**: rules persist long after conditions change because rule-mix evolution is slow.
- Uniquely evolutionary at the **population level**, not just agent level.

→ Anchor: **P·Bergmann (1974)**

nodes.title: P·Neugart (2008) — Discrete-Choice ABM
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Neugart, M. (2008). Labor market policy evaluation with ACE. *Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization*, 67(2), 418–430.

---

## Intro

Integrates McFadden's (1974) **discrete-choice** toolkit into labor-market ABM. Every agent decision (accept job, take training, hire applicant) is a multinomial logit with coefficients estimated from German micro-data (SOEP, LFS, IAB).

## What it adds to Bergmann (1974)

Bergmann's rules were arbitrary heuristics. Neugart:
- **Empirically calibratable logit rules** — each coefficient has an economic meaning pinned by observed choices.
- **Bridge between econometrics and ABM** — empirically-anchored logit substitutes for optimization at O(J) per agent per period.

## Results

- Reproduces policy-response magnitudes matching natural-experiment estimates for training subsidies and UI changes.
- Established the **empirical-anchor standard** for labor ABMs.

→ Anchor: **P·Bergmann (1974)** → extends to **P·Martin–Neugart (2009)** (DC for wage-setting)

nodes.title: P·Martin–Neugart (2009) — DC for Wage-Setting
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Martin, C. & Neugart, M. (2009). Shocks, endogenous rigidity, and the role of a shock-absorbing labor market institution. *Applied Economics*, 41(9), 1141–1153.

---

## Intro

Extends Neugart 2008's discrete-choice ABM from **policy-participation** decisions to the **transactional core** of the labor market — wage-setting, turnover, hiring/firing.

## What it adds to Neugart (2008)

Neugart 2008 handled accept-training-yes/no decisions. MN 2009:
- **Firm posts vacancy? Hire? Wage offer?** All logit choices.
- **Worker accept? Quit?** All logit choices.
- Institutional features (UI, short-time work, wage subsidies) enter as $V$-shifts.

## Results

- **Full labor-market equilibrium** from discrete choice alone — no Nash bargaining, no wage posting.
- **Institutional shock-absorbers** cut cyclical amplitude by 15–30% in calibrated model.

→ Anchor: **P·Neugart (2008)**

nodes.title: P·Richiardi (2006) — Adaptive TD Learning
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Richiardi, M. (2006). Toward a non-equilibrium unemployment theory. *Computational Economics*, 27(1), 135–160.

---

## Intro

Replaces the McCall/Mortensen–Pissarides Bellman-equation for reservation wage with the **simplest possible learning primitive**: temporal-difference (TD) updating.

## What it adds to Bergmann (1974)

Bergmann had fixed rules. Richiardi:
- Workers keep a running $\hat V_{\text{search}}$ (perceived value of searching).
- Decide via reservation-payoff test.
- Update: $\hat V \leftarrow \hat V + \alpha(\text{realized} - \hat V)$.
- Rule stays fixed; the parameter evolves with experience.

## Results

- Converges to near-optimal search without computing a value function.
- **Persistent non-equilibrium unemployment** — new workers keep entering and learning from scratch, so the aggregate never fully settles.
- **Hysteresis** — shocks leave lasting marks that closed-form models rule out by stationarity assumption.

→ Anchor: **P·Bergmann (1974)** → extends to **P·Gemkow–Neugart (2011)** (Q-learning + networks)

nodes.title: P·Gemkow–Neugart (2011) — RL + Networks
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Gemkow, S. & Neugart, M. (2011). Referral hiring, endogenous social networks, and inequality: an agent-based analysis. *Journal of Evolutionary Economics*, 21, 703–719.

---

## Intro

Extends Richiardi's TD to a **richer state–action space**: how much to invest in maintaining each social tie, given uncertain and delayed referral payoffs.

## What it adds to Richiardi (2006)

Richiardi's TD was scalar (search or not). GN:
- **Q-table over network-investment actions**.
- **Softmax exploration** — occasionally picks suboptimal actions (necessary when payoff landscape isn't monotonic).
- **Endogenous networks** — ties decay if not maintained; new ties form via matching.

## Results

- **Endogenous inequality from cumulative advantage.** Two ex-ante identical workers diverge: early luck → high Q → more investment → more referrals; early failure → disengagement → cumulative disadvantage.
- **First serious use of Q-learning in labor economics** — imports RL from AI without pretending agents are hyper-rational.

→ Anchor: **P·Richiardi (2006)**

nodes.title: P·Boudreau (2010) — Rank-Based Imitation
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Boudreau, J. (2010). Rank-based rules and workforce decisions in agent-based models.

---

## Intro

At the opposite end of the ABM design spectrum from RL: the **fixed heuristic**. Worker imitates the person ranked immediately above them (Festinger 1954 social comparison).

## What it adds to Bergmann (1974)

Bergmann's OR rules were mechanical. Boudreau:
- **Rank-based imitation** — a documented behavioural pattern.
- No learning parameters, no logit coefficients — a static rule.

## Results

- Emergent inequality from a minimal rule: stratification, path dependence, realistic right tail.
- Schelling-style demonstration: minimal rules → non-obvious aggregate outcomes.
- **Provides the field's null model** — every richer decision rule must beat rank imitation to earn its complexity.

→ Anchor: **P·Bergmann (1974)**

nodes.title: P·ML3 (Reinhardt–Warnke–Uhrmacher 2022) — Methodology
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Reinhardt, O., Warnke, T. & Uhrmacher, A. M. (2022). A formal foundation for the modeling language ML3. *ACM Transactions on Modeling and Computer Simulation*, 32(1), Article 6.

---

## Intro

**Domain-specific language** with rigorous mathematical semantics (Generalized Semi-Markov Process, GSMP) for **continuous-time, mixed-event agent-based simulations** — where some events are stochastic (fertility rates), some deterministic (retirement at 65), some periodic (monthly reviews).

## Why it matters

Solves what NetLogo/Mesa (discrete-time only), PRISM/CTMC (memoryless only), and DEVS (over-hierarchical) all handle awkwardly. Provides:
- **Reproducibility** — semantic equivalence across reimplementations.
- **Verification** — formal proofs of model properties.
- **Composition** — safe combination of sub-models.

## Where it fits

Methodology / infrastructure — not a substantive paper. Sits alongside the ABM tree as **how you'd build the next generation** of demographic + labor-market ABMs rigorously.

→ Anchor: methodology satellite of the ABM tree

nodes.title: P·Rivkin–Siggelkow (2003) — 3-Tier Hierarchy
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Rivkin, J. & Siggelkow, N. (2003). Balancing search and stability: Interdependencies among elements of organizational design. *Management Science*, 49(3), 290–311.

---

## Intro

Rare published **three-tier organizational ABM**: workers × middle managers × top. Middle managers as active agents (filters and amplifiers), not passive conduits.

## What it adds to Levinthal (1997)

Levinthal's NK model had a **single-tier** firm searching a landscape. Rivkin–Siggelkow add:
- **Three explicit agent types** — workers, middle managers (propose+filter), top (approve+override).
- **Middle-manager filter rules** as a first-class design parameter (span of control, filter strictness).
- **Search-vs-stability tradeoff** formalized: loose delegation → oscillation; strict filtering → convergence but slow adaptation.

## Results

- Optimal span of control ≈ 5–15 emerges from NK dynamics — matches management-consulting rules of thumb.
- Turbulent environments favour loose hierarchies; stable environments favour strict filtering.

→ Anchor: **P·Levinthal (1997)**

nodes.title: P·Levinthal (1997) — NK Landscapes
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Levinthal, D. A. (1997). Adaptation on rugged landscapes. *Management Science*, 43(7), 934–950.

---

## Intro

**Founding paper of NK-landscape organizational simulation.** Imports Kauffman's (1993) NK model from evolutionary biology to explain persistent firm heterogeneity from identical starts.

## What it adds to Bergmann (1974)

Bergmann's firms had no strategic-choice landscape. Levinthal:
- **Firm = N binary policy choices** with K-degree interdependencies.
- **Rugged fitness landscape** — modest K → multiple local optima.
- **Local search + occasional long jumps** — models exploration vs exploitation (March 1991) computationally.

## Results

- **Path-dependent firm heterogeneity** from identical starts.
- **Formalizes exploration-vs-exploitation** as a landscape-ruggedness tradeoff.
- **Founding paper** of the NK-strategy literature — every subsequent org-simulation (Rivkin–Siggelkow, Siggelkow–Levinthal, Ethiraj–Levinthal, Chang–Harrington) builds on this base.

→ Anchor: **P·Bergmann (1974)** (methodologically) → extends to **P·Rivkin–Siggelkow (2003)** (adds hierarchy)

nodes.title: P·Neugart–Richiardi (2018) — Handbook Synthesis
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Neugart, M. & Richiardi, M. (2018). Agent-based models of the labor market. In *Handbook of Computational Economics, Vol. 4* (Cars Hommes & Blake LeBaron, eds.). Elsevier / North-Holland.

---

## Intro

**Definitive field survey.** Written by two of the most productive practitioners. Serves as the roadmap for anyone building a labor-market ABM.

## What it adds

- **Taxonomy on 4 axes**: agent decision rule (fixed / DC / adaptive / RL / optimizing), market focus, calibration strategy, validation target.
- **Best-practice design patterns**: modular architecture, RNG seeding, sensitivity sweeps.
- **Gap list** — actionable open problems. First one: integrated incentive-alternative ABMs with per-contract identification.
- **Validation criteria** — how to demonstrate the ABM is credible.

## Contribution

Establishes field identity. First citation in any subsequent labor-market ABM paper.

→ Anchor: labor branch synthesis of **P·Bergmann (1974)** lineage

nodes.title: P·Ross (1973) — Agency Problem
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Ross, S. A. (1973). The economic theory of agency: The principal's problem. *American Economic Review*, 63(2), 134–139.

---

## Intro

The **founding statement** of the principal-agent problem. Formalises the delegation of choice from principal to agent under asymmetric information and misaligned incentives.

## Contribution

- Defines the **agent's utility** and the **principal's problem** as separate optimization objects.
- Shows the principal must design a contract $w(y)$ that induces the agent to act in the principal's interest despite the agent's private information.
- Establishes the concept of **incentive compatibility**.

## Position

Under **①** raw agency problem. First theoretical statement.

nodes.title: P·Mirrlees (1975/1999) — Moral Hazard
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Mirrlees, J. A. (1975 WP; 1999). The theory of moral hazard and unobservable behaviour. *Review of Economic Studies*, 66(1), 3–21.

---

## Intro

The formal foundation of **moral hazard**. Generalizes Ross 1973 to a fully-specified statistical decision problem.

## Contribution

- Frames the PA problem as: choose the wage function $w(y)$ to maximize principal's expected payoff subject to (i) the agent's participation constraint and (ii) the agent's incentive-compatibility constraint (agent chooses effort to maximize their own utility given the contract).
- **Sufficient-statistic result:** the optimal wage depends only on those signals informative about effort — direct precursor to Holmström 1979.

## Position

Under **①** raw agency problem. Establishes the mathematical setup used by every downstream paper.

→ Anchor: extends to **P·Holmström (1979)** (informativeness principle)

nodes.title: P·Holmström (1979) — Informativeness
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Holmström, B. (1979). Moral hazard and observability. *Bell Journal of Economics*, 10(1), 74–91.

---

## Intro

Establishes the **informativeness principle** — the theoretical foundation for why gathering more information about effort raises welfare.

## Contribution

- A signal $s$ should be included in the wage contract **if and only if it carries information about effort beyond what's already in $y$**.
- Formally: $s$ enters the optimal contract iff the conditional distribution $p(y|e)$ depends on $s$.
- **Sufficient-statistic characterization**: the optimal wage $w^*(y, s)$ depends on $(y,s)$ only through a sufficient statistic for effort.

## Why it matters for Quindi

This IS the theoretical justification for information-technology solutions to agency:
- Every new informative signal Quindi provides shifts $\beta^*$ up (HM 1987) and reduces the risk premium.
- Quindi is doing Holmström-1979-approved work: it's providing signals correlated with effort.

## Position

Green **②** — direct theoretical support for information-based solutions.

nodes.title: P·Grossman–Hart (1983) — General PA
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Grossman, S. J. & Hart, O. D. (1983). An analysis of the principal-agent problem. *Econometrica*, 51(1), 7–45.

---

## Intro

**General characterization** of the optimal contract in the finite-action PA problem — without the CARA/Gaussian assumptions of HM 1987.

## Contribution

- Two-step decomposition:
  1. **Implementation cost** $C(a)$ — the minimum expected wage bill to implement action $a$.
  2. **Optimal action** — the one that maximizes $E[y | a] - C(a)$.
- Characterizes when the optimal $w(y)$ is monotone in $y$ (needs MLRP — monotone likelihood ratio property).

## Position

Green **②** — general theoretical framework that HM 1987's linear contract is a special case of.

nodes.title: P·Holmström–Milgrom (1987) — Linear Contract
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Holmström, B. & Milgrom, P. (1987). Aggregation and linearity in the provision of intertemporal incentives. *Econometrica*, 55(2), 303–328.

---

## Intro

Delivers the **optimal linear contract theorem** — the workhorse of applied incentive theory.

## Setup

- Continuous-time output $dY_t = a_t\,dt + \sigma\,dW_t$.
- CARA utility for the agent.
- Effort cost $c(a) = ka^2/2$.

## Result

Two miracles:
- **Aggregation**: nothing is gained by paying separately for every fluctuation; only cumulative $Y_T$ matters.
- **Linearity**: the optimal contract is exactly $w = \alpha + \beta Y_T$ — not approximately.

The optimal slope:
$$\boxed{\;\beta^* = \frac{1}{1 + \rho\sigma^2 k / g'^{\,2}}\;}$$

- $\rho\uparrow$ or $\sigma^2\uparrow$: $\beta^*$ falls.
- $g'\uparrow$ (signal more informative about effort): $\beta^*$ rises.

## Position

Green **②** solution to raw agency. Foundation of applied incentive theory.

nodes.title: P·Lazear–Rosen (1981) — Tournaments
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Lazear, E. P. & Rosen, S. (1981). Rank-order tournaments as optimum labor contracts. *Journal of Political Economy*, 89(5), 841–864.

---

## Intro

**Founding paper of tournament theory.** Answers: when should a firm pay workers by RANK instead of by cardinal output?

## Setup

$N$ agents choose effort $e_i$ at cost $c(e_i) = ke_i^2/2$. Output $y_i = e_i + \varepsilon_i$. Prizes $w_H$ (winner) and $w_L$ (loser). Spread $\Delta = w_H - w_L$.

## Derivation

Win probability: $P_i^{\text{win}} = G(\mu(e_i) - \mu(e_j))$ where $G$ is the CDF of $\xi = \varepsilon_j - \varepsilon_i$.

Symmetric equilibrium IC:
$$\Delta \cdot \mu'(e^*) \cdot g_\xi(0) = c'(e^*)$$

Under Gaussian noise + linear $\mu$ + quadratic $c$:
$$\boxed{\;e^* = \frac{\Delta}{k\sigma\sqrt{4\pi}}\;}$$

Under risk-neutrality, setting $\Delta^* = \sigma\sqrt{4\pi}$ implements first-best effort exactly.

## Contribution

- Formalizes rank-order pay.
- **First-best under risk-neutrality.**
- Genuine advantage: **common-noise filtering** — ranks are invariant to $\eta$ (Nalebuff–Stiglitz 1983).

## Position

Green **④** — theoretical foundation. Empirical descendants below (EB 1990, CAMJ 2009, Kolstad 2013).

---

## Contract-family view (A2 Tournament / Rank-Order Contest)

## A2 · Tournament / Rank-Order Contest

Replace flat wage $w_0$ with rank-based prizes: winner $w_H$, loser $w_L$, spread $\Delta = w_H - w_L$. Worker's problem:
$$\max_{e_i}\; \Delta \cdot P_i(\text{win} \mid e_i, e_{-i}) - c(e_i).$$

IC condition at symmetric equilibrium:
$$\Delta \cdot \mu'(e^*) \cdot g_\xi(0) = c'(e^*).$$

**Solves**: F1 (measurement) via common-shock cancellation; F3 (ratchet).   **Breaks**: sabotage, collusion, F5 (cooperation), late-round risk-taking distortion.

**See [[P·Lazear–Rosen (1981) — Tournaments]]** for the full 7-step derivation, first-best result under risk-neutrality, common-noise dominance argument, and all references.

nodes.title: P·Holmström (1982) — Career Concerns
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Holmström, B. (1982 WP; 1999). Managerial incentive problems: A dynamic perspective. *Review of Economic Studies*, 66(1), 169–182.

---

## Intro

**Founding paper of career-concerns theory.** Complements Fama 1980 by giving the short-run signal-jamming mechanism.

## Setup

- Manager's ability $\theta$ unknown. Output $y_t = \theta + e_t + \varepsilon_t$.
- Competitive labor market pays $w_t = \mathbb{E}[\theta | y_1, ..., y_{t-1}]$.

## Result — signal-jamming FOC

Manager's effort satisfies:
$$\delta \cdot \sum_{\tau=t+1}^{T} \delta^{\tau-t-1} \cdot \frac{\sigma^2_t}{\sigma^2_t + \sigma^2} = k e_t$$

- **Early career effort is high** — high uncertainty $\sigma_t^2$ about ability → market puts high weight on signal.
- **Late-career effort declines** — market learns $\theta$, weight collapses.

## Position

Green **② (alt.)** — theoretical foundation for career-concerns effort. Empirically supported by observed age–effort profiles.

nodes.title: P·Fama (1980) — Implicit Incentives via Labor Market
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Fama, E. F. (1980). Agency problems and the theory of the firm. *Journal of Political Economy*, 88(2), 288–307.

---

## Intro

Argues that **the market for managers itself provides the incentives** the agency literature worries about — no explicit contract is needed.

## Claim

- Manager's ability is inferred from past performance over the career.
- Next-period wage tracks the market's revised belief about ability.
- In the long run, PV of future wage adjustments = PV of current output → agency problem solved WITHOUT explicit performance pay.

## Position

Green **② (alt.)** — implicit incentives from career concerns, no formal contract required. Complements Holmström 1982's short-run signal-jamming model.

nodes.title: P·Shapiro–Stiglitz (1984) — Efficiency Wage
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Shapiro, C. & Stiglitz, J. E. (1984). Equilibrium unemployment as a worker discipline device. *American Economic Review*, 74(3), 433–444.

---

## Intro

**Efficiency-wage microfoundation** for involuntary unemployment.

## Setup

- Continuous time. Effort $e \in \{0, 1\}$.
- If shirking, caught with Poisson intensity $q$; if caught, fired.
- Fired workers enter unemployment; find new job at rate $a$; earn UI $\bar w$.

## No-shirking condition

Worker chooses not to shirk iff:
$$\boxed{\; w = \bar w + c + \frac{c(r + a + b)}{q} \;}$$

Firms must pay $w > w^{MC}$ (efficiency wage). Equilibrium unemployment IS the discipline device — it makes losing the job costly.

## Position

Green **② (alt.)** — a non-linear alternative solution to the raw agency problem. Discipline via threat of unemployment, not via output-contingent pay.

---

## Contract-family view (A3 Fixed Wage + Efficiency Wage)

### How this modifies the base model

Keep $w_0 > w^{MC}$ (as in Weiss) **plus** monitoring probability $q$ + dismissal on detected shirking.

**Shapiro–Stiglitz no-shirking condition**:
$$w_0 - w^{MC} \;\geq\; \frac{c(e)\,(1-\delta)}{q\,\delta}$$

Wage premium must exceed effort cost adjusted by monitoring intensity. $e_i^{*} > 0$ induced by threat of losing the rent — not by output linkage.

---

**Signal**: none directly — pay is flat. Motivation from *threat of dismissal* under monitoring, plus wage above market-clearing so the job is worth keeping.

**Solves**
- Removes all output-based risk (F4).
- No metric to game → attacks multitasking (F2), Goodhart (F6).
- No incentive to hoard output → attacks cooperation collapse (F5).

**Breaks**
- Requires credible monitoring AND credible dismissal.
- Involuntary unemployment as equilibrium feature.
- No high-powered incentive → productivity ceiling.

**Use when**: output signals noisy or gameable; quality > quantity; firm has monitoring infrastructure.

---

### References

- **Shapiro, C. & Stiglitz, J. (1984)**. Equilibrium unemployment as a worker discipline device. *AER*, 74(3), 433–444.
- **Yellen, J. (1984)**. Efficiency wage models of unemployment. *AER Papers & Proceedings*, 74(2), 200–205 (survey).
- **Salop, S. (1979)**. A model of the natural rate of unemployment. *AER*, 69(1), 117–125 (turnover-cost variant).
- **Akerlof, G. (1982)**. Labor contracts as partial gift exchange. *QJE*, 97(4), 543–569.
- **Bulow, J. & Summers, L. (1986)**. A theory of dual labor markets. *Journal of Labor Economics*, 4(3), 376–414.
- **Krueger, A. & Summers, L. (1988)**. Efficiency wages and the inter-industry wage structure. *Econometrica*, 56(2), 259–293 (evidence).

nodes.title: P·Baker–Gibbons–Murphy (1994) — Subjective Evaluation
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Baker, G., Gibbons, R. & Murphy, K. J. (1994). Subjective performance measures in optimal incentive contracts. *Quarterly Journal of Economics*, 109(4), 1125–1156.

---

## Intro

**Foundational paper on relational-contract incentives.** Firms use both objective (verifiable) signals and subjective (unverifiable) supervisor ratings. Standard PA theory (Holmström 1979) says use only verifiable signals. BGM ask: when is the subjective signal worth using despite non-contractibility?

## Setup

Wage: $w = \alpha + \beta y + b(m)$
- $y$: verifiable but distorted (noisy or misaligned — multi-tasking).
- $m$: subjective, precise, but unverifiable.
- $b$: discretionary bonus at firm's discretion.

## Credibility constraint

Firm cannot be forced to pay $b$ ex-post. So bonus is credible only if:
$$b \leq \delta \cdot V^{\text{future}}_{\text{firm}}$$

Firm's future rents must exceed the temptation to renege.

## Result

- When $y$ is heavily distorted (multi-tasking) or noisy, the firm rationally uses the subjective bonus even at credibility cost.
- Explains empirical bonus structures (mixed objective + subjective).
- Foundation for the relational-contract literature (Baker–Gibbons–Murphy 2002; MacLeod 2003; Levin 2003).

## Position

Green **⑥** — theoretical foundation for subjective evaluation.

nodes.title: P·MacLeod (2003) — Relational Contracts w/ Subjective Eval
nodes.content:
**Ref.** MacLeod, W. B. (2003). Optimal contracting with subjective evaluation. *American Economic Review*, 93(1), 216–240.

---

## Intro

Provides the **complete characterization** of when subjective evaluation is credible in an equilibrium sense — MacLeod formalizes the intuition BGM 1994 introduced.

## Setup

- Manager privately observes rating $m$ correlated with worker's effort.
- Rating unverifiable by third parties.
- Bonus $b$ paid iff manager reports $m = H$.
- Repeated relationship, discount $\delta$.

## Truth-telling constraint

Manager truthfully reports $m$ iff:
$$b \leq \delta \cdot V^{\text{future}}_{\text{firm}}$$

## Trigger strategy

If manager ever reports $\hat m \neq m$, worker triggers permanent effort withdrawal → firm loses all future rents.

## Result

- Subjective evaluation sustains high effort IF the firm's future rent stream is credible.
- **Reputation for fairness** — sustained by rational trigger strategies from workers.

## Position

Green **⑥** — completes the theoretical foundation for subjective evaluation with a full equilibrium characterization.

---

## Contract-family view (A7 Subjective Evaluation + Bonus)

### How this modifies the base model

Manager privately observes rating $m_i$ correlated with effort. Bonus $b(m_i)$ on top of $w_0$:
$$w_i = w_0 + b(m_i)$$

Worker's effort FOC:
$$\mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{\partial b(m_i)}{\partial e_i}\right] = c'(e_i^{*})$$

Optimal $b^{*}$ (MacLeod 2003) balances effort inducement against **influence-activity** cost. Requires a **relational contract**: manager must credibly commit not to renege; reneging destroys the equilibrium.

---

**Signal**: manager's private assessment, converted to bonus/promotion.

**Solves**
- Manager can down-weight lucky outcomes and reward true effort → attacks measurement noise (F1).
- Rewards multi-dim performance → attacks multitasking (F2).
- Preserves flexibility to reward cooperation, culture, mentoring (F5).
- No explicit threshold → no bunching (F6).

**Breaks**
- Influence activities (Milgrom 1988): workers persuade the manager instead of producing.
- Favoritism, discrimination, arbitrary variation.
- Requires a **relational contract**: manager must credibly commit to fair evaluation (MacLeod 2003).
- Legally hard to defend if evaluations diverge from measurables.

**Use when**: output is complex, multi-dimensional, hard to game via explicit metrics; long employment relationships with repeated interaction.

---

### References

- **MacLeod, W. B. (2003)**. Optimal contracting with subjective evaluation. *AER*, 93(1), 216–240.
- **Baker, G., Gibbons, R. & Murphy, K. J. (1994)**. Subjective performance measures in optimal incentive contracts. *QJE*, 109(4), 1125–1156.
- **Milgrom, P. (1988)**. Employment contracts, influence activities, and efficient organization design. *JPE*, 96(1), 42–60.
- **Prendergast, C. & Topel, R. (1996)**. Favoritism in organizations. *JPE*, 104(5), 958–978.
- **Levin, J. (2003)**. Relational incentive contracts. *AER*, 93(3), 835–857.
- **Prendergast, C. (2002)**. The tenuous trade-off between risk and incentives. *JPE*, 110(5), 1071–1102.

nodes.title: P·Kandel–Lazear (1992) — Peer Pressure
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Kandel, E. & Lazear, E. P. (1992). Peer pressure and partnerships. *Journal of Political Economy*, 100(4), 801–817.

---

## Intro

**Founding paper of peer-pressure theory.** Explains a puzzle: partnerships (law firms, medical practices, investment banks) share revenue equally among partners, yet Holmström 1982's team-moral-hazard theorem says free-riding should collapse effort as team size grows. Why do these organizations thrive?

## Setup

Team of $N$ partners under equal-sharing team pay. Effort $e_i$ produces output $y_i = g e_i$. Peer-pressure cost $\psi(e_i, \bar e_{-i})$ with $\psi_1 < 0$ (higher own effort reduces shame cost) and $\psi_2 > 0$ (higher peer effort raises shame cost of shirking).

## FOC

$$\frac{g}{N} - c'(e_i) - \psi_1(e_i, \bar e_{-i}) = 0$$

Peer pressure ADDS $-\psi_1 > 0$ to the effort incentive. If peer pressure exceeds free-rider dilution ($1/N$-vs-$1$ marginal-return gap), team pay dominates individual pay.

## Position

Green **⑥** — theoretical foundation for team pay + peer monitoring.

---

## Contract-family view (A4 Team Pay / Profit Sharing)

### How this modifies the base model

Add group-signal slope on top of $w_0$:
$$w_i = w_0 + \beta_T \cdot s_{\text{team}}, \quad s_{\text{team}} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^N y_j$$

Marginal own-effort incentive:
$$\frac{\partial w_i}{\partial e_i} = \frac{\beta_T}{N}$$

Free-rider scales with $N$: individual reward on own effort $\propto 1/N$.

Kandel–Lazear (1992): peer pressure supplements the $1/N$ direct incentive for small $N$ — worker $i$ internalizes some cost of others' scrutiny.

---

**Signal**: group-level output — team quota, plant profits, firm profit.

**Solves**
- Rewards cooperation, mentoring, mutual help directly (F5).
- Aligns worker to firm value → attacks narrow-metric multitasking (F2).
- Peer pressure polices free-riders in small teams (Kandel–Lazear).

**Breaks**
- Free-rider problem grows with N — marginal reward on effort ≈ 1/N.
- Requires observability *between* peers so social pressure operates.
- Loads systematic risk (firm-wide shocks) onto workers — WORSENS F4.

**Use when**: small tight teams with strong cooperation externalities and mutual observability (surgical team, small startup).

---

### References

- **Kandel, E. & Lazear, E. (1992)**. Peer pressure and partnerships. *JPE*, 100(4), 801–817.
- **Weitzman, M. & Kruse, D. (1990)**. Profit sharing and productivity. In *Paying for Productivity*, Brookings.
- **Alchian, A. & Demsetz, H. (1972)**. Production, information costs, and economic organization. *AER*, 62(5), 777–795.
- **Holmström, B. (1982)**. Moral hazard in teams. *Bell JE*, 13(2), 324–340 (free-rider theorem).
- **Hamilton, B., Nickerson, J. & Owan, H. (2003)**. Team incentives and worker heterogeneity. *JPE*, 111(3), 465–497.
- **Bandiera, O., Barankay, I. & Rasul, I. (2013)**. Team incentives: evidence from a firm level experiment. *JEEA*, 11(5), 1079–1114.

nodes.title: P·Gibbons (1987) — Ratchet Effect
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Gibbons, R. (1987). Piece-rate incentive schemes. *Journal of Labor Economics*, 5(4), 413–429.

---

## Intro

Formalizes the **ratchet effect** in the PA framework — workers strategically under-produce today to keep tomorrow's target favourable.

## Setup

- Two periods.
- Worker's ability $\theta$ private.
- Firm can't commit to period-2 contract; updates target from period-1 output.

## Result

High-ability worker's period-1 effort satisfies
$$k \cdot e_1^* = \beta_1 \theta_H + \delta \cdot \underbrace{\partial \pi_2 / \partial \hat p}_{<0} \cdot \underbrace{\partial \hat p / \partial e_1}_{>0}$$

so $e_1^* < e^{\text{one-shot}}$. **Strategic under-production.**

## Position

Red **③** — another residual problem. Motivates:
- **Yardstick competition** (Holmström 1982; Shleifer 1985) — compare to peer output, not own history.
- **Commitment devices** (Laffont–Tirole 1988) — long-term contracts.

---

## Failure-mode view (F3 Ratchet Effect)

**Problem**

Worker hides capacity — puts low effort in easy periods so the firm doesn't discover the task is easy and raise the quota next period. Roy (1952); Bandiera–Barankay–Rasul (2005).

**Mechanism**
Worker's optimal effort today depends on how effort maps to *tomorrow's target*, not just today's pay. High output today → tighter quota tomorrow → dampen output.

**Classical fix (Holmström 1982; Shleifer 1985)**
Index quota to *peers*, not own history — own effort no longer feeds own standard. Yardstick competition. This is essentially A2 Tournament.

**Which alternatives address it**
- A2 Tournament (peer-indexed quotas)
- A5 Deferred comp (long horizon dilutes ratchet gain)
- A6 Career concerns (market has no reason to raise your standard)

---

### References

- **Gibbons, R. (1987)**. Piece-rate incentive schemes. *Journal of Labor Economics*, 5(4), 413–429.
- **Roy, D. (1952)**. Quota restriction and goldbricking in a machine shop. *American Journal of Sociology*, 57(5), 427–442.
- **Weitzman, M. (1980)**. The 'ratchet principle' and performance incentives. *Bell JE*, 11(1), 302–308 (Soviet planning context).
- **Bandiera, O., Barankay, I. & Rasul, I. (2007)**. Incentives for managers and inequality among workers: evidence from a firm-level experiment. *QJE*, 122(2), 729–773.
- **Holmström, B. (1982)**. Moral hazard in teams. *Bell JE*, 13(2), 324–340 (yardstick / peer benchmark).
- **Shleifer, A. (1985)**. A theory of yardstick competition. *RAND JE*, 16(3), 319–327.
- **Freixas, X., Guesnerie, R. & Tirole, J. (1985)**. Planning under incomplete information and the ratchet effect. *REStud*, 52(2), 173–191.

nodes.title: P·Hamilton–Nickerson–Owan (2003) — Cooperation Collapse
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Hamilton, B. H., Nickerson, J. A. & Owan, H. (2003). Team incentives and worker heterogeneity: An empirical analysis of the impact of teams on productivity and participation. *Journal of Political Economy*, 111(3), 465–497.

---

## Intro

**First large-N empirical decomposition** of team-vs-individual pay in a garment plant that switched to team pay in the early 1990s.

## Findings

- **Team productivity ~14% higher than individual productivity** on the same workers — REVERSING the Holmström 1982 free-rider prediction.
- Decomposition: ~60% peer effects, ~40% ability sorting.
- Shows that when individual pay was used, workers didn't share knowledge or help each other — cooperation had collapsed.

## Position

Red **⑤** in the "diagnosis" sense: piece rate / rank pay had killed cooperation.
Green **⑥** in the "solution" sense: switching to team pay REVERSED the collapse.

Bridging card that motivates the ⑥ green solutions.

---

## Failure-mode view (F5 Cooperation Collapse)

**Evidence**
Garment plant switched from team pay to individual piece rates → total output FELL despite rising individual effort. Workers stopped teaching, helping, covering. Also Encinosa–Gaynor–Rebitzer (2007) on physician groups.

**Mechanism**
Under piece rates, time spent helping a peer = zero personal reward + opportunity cost of your own output. Rational response: withdraw from cooperation. Knowledge transfer disappears.

**Which alternatives address it**
- A3 Fixed wage (nothing to compete over)
- A4 Team pay (directly rewards cooperation)
- A7 Subjective (manager rewards mentoring)
- A8 Ownership (residual claim on joint output)

**Which alternatives make it WORSE**
- A2 Tournament (helping a peer is directly costly)

---

### References

- **Hamilton, B., Nickerson, J. & Owan, H. (2003)**. Team incentives and worker heterogeneity: garment plant evidence. *JPE*, 111(3), 465–497.
- **Encinosa, W., Gaynor, M. & Rebitzer, J. (2007)**. The sociology of groups and the economics of incentives. *JEBO*, 62(2), 187–214.
- **Bandiera, O., Barankay, I. & Rasul, I. (2005)**. Social preferences and the response to incentives. *QJE*, 120(3), 917–962 (peer effects).
- **Bandiera, O., Barankay, I. & Rasul, I. (2010)**. Social incentives in the workplace. *REStud*, 77(2), 417–458.
- **Freeman, R. & Medoff, J. (1984)**. *What Do Unions Do?* Basic Books (cooperation-through-voice).

nodes.title: P·Prendergast (1999) — Field Survey
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Prendergast, C. (1999). The provision of incentives in firms. *Journal of Economic Literature*, 37(1), 7–63.

---

## Intro

**Field-defining survey** of the incentives literature circa 1999. Positions Prendergast's own empirical work on the $\beta^*$-vs-$\sigma$ puzzle.

## Structure

Reviews:
- **Explicit incentives** (piece rates, tournaments, efficiency wages, back-loaded pay).
- **Implicit incentives** (career concerns, promotion tournaments, yardstick competition).
- **Non-monetary incentives** (peer pressure, subjective evaluation, multitasking).

## Key puzzle

- HM 1987 predicts $\beta^*$ falls in $\sigma^2$.
- Empirical work shows the relationship is **weak or wrong-signed**.

## Resolutions

1. **Delegation of decision rights** (Prendergast 2000, 2002 follow-ups).
2. **Multi-tasking distortion** (HM 1991).
3. **Subjective evaluation** (BGM 1994).
4. **Sample selection** — firms that survive with high-$\beta$ in high-$\sigma$ environments are the ones we observe.

## Position

Meta — starting citation for anyone entering personnel economics. Complements the presentation's narrative flow with the field's own self-understanding.

---

## Further reading (user notes)

**Original notes (verbatim):**

Search: Gibbons and Waldman (1999), Malcomson (1999), Prendergast (1999), Murphy (1999), and Lazear (1999, 2000b).

nodes.title: P·Ehrenberg–Bognanno (1990) — PGA Empirics
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Ehrenberg, R. G. & Bognanno, M. L. (1990). Do tournaments have incentive effects? *Journal of Political Economy*, 98(6), 1307–1324.

---

## Intro

**First empirical test of LR 1981.** Uses professional golf — the PGA circuit — as a natural laboratory. Real-world tournaments explicitly pay rank-ordered prizes.

## Design

- Panel of 1984 PGA + 1987 European PGA events.
- Player × tournament × round observations.
- Regress final-round score on prize spread, with player + course fixed effects.

## Findings

- **Bigger prize spread → significantly lower (better) final-round scores.**
- A $100k increase in top-4 spread lowers final-round score by ~1 stroke.
- Effects concentrated on **final round** — where the marginal probability of catching leaders is highest (exactly the LR 1981 interaction).

## Contribution

- First empirical confirmation of the prize-spread → effort mechanism.
- **Established the PGA as the canonical natural laboratory** for tournament theory.

nodes.title: P·Bandiera–Barankay–Rasul (2005) — Fruit-Picker Peer Effects
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Bandiera, O., Barankay, I. & Rasul, I. (2005). Social preferences and the response to incentives: Evidence from personnel data. *Quarterly Journal of Economics*, 120(3), 917–962.

---

## Intro

Empirical evidence that **social preferences** interact with the contract's payoff structure — a foundational empirical paper for personnel economics.

## Design

- UK soft-fruit farm; 142 workers × 108 field-days.
- **Mid-season switch** from relative incentives (piece rate deflated by field-day average) to individual piece rates.

## Findings

- **Productivity rose ~50%** after switching FROM relative pay TO individual piece rates.
- The gap was **largest for workers picking near friends** — social ties amplified the negative externality of relative pay on effort.
- Under relative pay, working harder hurt friends' pay via the deflator → workers internalized this and worked less.

## Contribution

Under **⑤** (red — problem): relative pay hurts effort when social ties are strong.

Under **⑥** (yellow — evidence): sets up the "social preferences interact with contracts" theme that BBR 2013 (below in ⑥) completes.

nodes.title: P·Casas-Arce–Martínez-Jerez (2009) — Sales Tournaments
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Casas-Arce, P. & Martínez-Jerez, F. A. (2009). Relative performance compensation, contests, and dynamic incentives. *Management Science*, 55(8), 1306–1320.

---

## Intro

Empirical test of LR 1981 in a **sales-force setting** with dynamic within-tournament data.

## Design

- Panel of ~2,000 salespeople in a large Latin American consumer-goods firm.
- Monthly sales tournaments; bonus for top decile.
- Weekly frequency data.

## Findings

- **Inverted-U in effort as a function of interim distance from the threshold.** Workers "on the bubble" exert most; front-runners coast; hopeless laggards give up.
- **Give-up threshold ~15%** (probability of catching up).
- **Coast threshold ~15%** (probability of losing lead).
- End-of-period effort resurgence as marginal returns shift.

## Contribution

Confirms **dynamic-contest** extension of LR 1981 (Rosen 1986; Ederer 2010). Provides actionable design implications — narrower brackets, mid-period reset — reduce give-up losses.

nodes.title: P·Bandiera–Barankay–Rasul (2013) — Team-Incentives Empirics
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Bandiera, O., Barankay, I. & Rasul, I. (2013). Team incentives: Evidence from a firm level experiment. *Journal of the European Economic Association*, 11(5), 1079–1114.

---

## Intro

**Follow-up field experiment** by BBR at the same UK fruit farm as BBR 2005 — but the OPPOSITE intervention. Where BBR 2005 compared individual relative vs individual piece rates, BBR 2013 compares individual piece vs TEAM piece with **endogenous team formation**.

## Design

- Workers randomly assigned to individual pay ($w = \beta y_i$) or team pay ($w = \beta \bar y_{\text{team}}$).
- **Endogenous team formation** — workers picked their own teammates. Team size 2–6.
- Same piece rate $\beta$ in both conditions.
- Within-worker variation across the season, absorbed by fixed effects.

## Findings

- **Team pay raised productivity ~10%** on the same workers — reversing the Holmström 1982 free-rider prediction.
- **Assortative matching** drove it: workers formed teams with friends + similar-ability peers.
- Decomposition: ~60% peer pressure, ~40% ability sorting.

## The two-sided BBR insight (with BBR 2005)

Same social ties = tax under tournaments (BBR 2005) = subsidy under team pay (BBR 2013). Contract structure determines sign.

## Position

Yellow **⑥** — empirical evidence for team-pay solution.

nodes.title: P·Kolstad (2013) — Surgeon Report Cards
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Kolstad, J. T. (2013). Information and quality when motivation is intrinsic: Evidence from surgeon report cards. *American Economic Review*, 103(7), 2875–2910.

---

## Intro

Tests LR 1981 in a **high-stakes hospital setting**. Uses New York State's Cardiac Surgery Reporting System (CSRS) — public rankings of cardiac-bypass surgeons by risk-adjusted mortality since 1991 — as a rank-order contest with **professional reputation** as the prize.

## Design

- ~450 surgeons across ~50 hospitals.
- Panel around the report-cards introduction.
- Structural decomposition of intrinsic (career-concerns) vs extrinsic (patient volume) channels.

## Findings

- **~10% reduction in risk-adjusted mortality** after report cards were introduced.
- **Intrinsic (career-concerns) channel ~4× larger than extrinsic (patient-volume) channel.** Fama-1980 / Holmström-1982 reputation dynamics dominate.
- Some multi-tasking / patient-selection concerns detected, but small relative to the quality gain.

## Contribution

- **Extends tournament theory to professional services** — the prize is reputation, not cash.
- Direct policy implication: public quality reporting can improve outcomes without any financial incentives tied to rank.

nodes.title: ★ Incentives Theory — Core
① PROBLEM · Raw Agency
nodes.content:
# ① The raw agency problem

**Effort is unobservable.**

The principal (firm) hires the agent (worker) to produce output $y$. Effort $e$ affects $y$ but is not directly seen. Any observable proxy is noisy:
$$y = g e + \varepsilon, \quad \varepsilon \sim (\text{noise})$$

Worker dislikes effort ($c(e)$ increasing convex). If wage is FLAT ($w = w_0$), worker chooses $e = 0$. This is the **moral hazard core problem** (Ross 1973; Mirrlees 1975).

Alchian & Demsetz (1972) reframed it as a **team-production monitoring** problem: firms exist as institutions that put someone (the residual claimant) in charge of monitoring effort in team settings where individual output isn't separately observable.

## What the papers below establish

- The formal PA setup and the impossibility of first-best.
- Alchian–Demsetz's team-production monitoring frame.

## What's needed next

A contract that **conditions wage on a noisy output signal** — and that we can characterize as *optimal* given the signal-noise structure. → **Green ②** (linear contract + info tracking).

nodes.title: P·Alchian–Demsetz (1972) — Team Production
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Alchian, A. A. & Demsetz, H. (1972). Production, information costs, and economic organization. *American Economic Review*, 62(5), 777–795.

---

## Intro

Reframes the raw agency problem as a **team-production monitoring** problem. Fundamental for understanding why firms exist as institutions distinct from markets.

## Contribution

- **Team production** ($y = f(e_1, e_2, ..., e_N)$ where individual $e_i$ aren't separately observable) creates a monitoring problem.
- The solution is to assign a **residual claimant** — someone who owns the profit after paying inputs, and therefore has the strongest incentive to monitor.
- This IS the classical firm: someone with residual-claim rights is the boss.

## Position

Under **①** raw agency problem. Complements Ross–Mirrlees by explaining WHY firms exist as institutional solutions to the agency problem (rather than pure market contracting).

nodes.title: ② SOLUTION · Linear Contract + Info Tracking
nodes.content:
# ② Linear contract + informative signals

**Reveal effort by conditioning wage on an informative signal.**

Under CARA + Gaussian noise, Holmström & Milgrom (1987) show the **optimal contract is exactly linear**:
$$w^* = \alpha + \beta \cdot y, \quad \beta^* = \frac{1}{1 + \rho \sigma^2 k / g^2}$$

- Higher risk-aversion $\rho$ → lower $\beta$ (worker can't bear risk).
- **Lower noise $\sigma^2$ → higher $\beta$ → more effort → higher first-best-share of surplus.**

**Holmström's (1979) informativeness principle**: use every signal that carries information about effort — the marginal benefit of adding an informative signal is always positive.

## Why Quindi fits here

Quindi's core business is **producing high-fidelity signals of worker effort** (green card next to this one). Every unit of noise reduction Quindi provides:
- Increases the optimal $\beta$.
- Reduces the risk premium the firm must pay to induce effort.
- Raises equilibrium output.

Quindi is **not a contract** — it is the substrate that makes every downstream contract better.

## What's needed next

Even with the best linear contract, agents bear residual noise. If $\sigma^2$ is large enough or shocks are **common** across agents (industry conditions, weather), the risk premium eats the surplus. → **Red ③** (idiosyncratic + common shocks).

nodes.title: ★ Quindi = Information Substrate
nodes.content:
# Quindi as the information substrate

**Quindi is not a contract. Quindi is the technology that makes every contract better.**

## The formal claim

Holmström & Milgrom (1987) prove the optimal linear contract is
$$w^* = \alpha + \beta y, \quad \beta^* = \frac{1}{1 + \rho\sigma^2 k / g^2}.$$

**Every $\sigma^2$-reducing intervention:**
- Raises $\beta^*$ (worker takes more of the residual).
- Raises equilibrium effort $e^* = \beta^* g / k$.
- Reduces the risk premium $\rho\sigma^2\beta^{*2}/2$ the firm must pay.
- Raises equilibrium output $\mathbb{E}[y^*]$ and firm profit.

## Quindi's business = reducing $\sigma^2$

Quindi's product produces high-frequency, high-fidelity signals of worker effort (task completion, activity metrics, output-quality proxies) that a firm's manager alone cannot cheaply observe.

Under Holmström's (1979) **informativeness principle**, each additional informative signal Quindi provides *should* enter the wage contract — improving welfare on both sides.

## Empirical grounding

- **Lazear 2000** (Safelite): switching to piece rate → 44% productivity gain. This is HM 1987 in the field, with clean signals of individual output. Quindi generalises the Safelite condition (clean individual signal) to industries where signals are noisier.
- **Bloom & Van Reenen 2013**: better management practices (largely = better measurement + info flow) → 17% productivity gain across 30k firms globally.

## The three empirical papers below (yellow)

Support the claim that better info + optimal linear contract raises productivity in a range of empirical settings.

→ Anchor: **P·Holmström–Milgrom (1987)** and **P·Holmström (1979)**

nodes.title: P·Lazear (2000) — Safelite Empirics
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Lazear, E. (2000). Performance pay and productivity. *American Economic Review*, 90(5), 1346–1361.

---

## Intro

The **canonical empirical benchmark** for piece-rate incentive effects in personnel economics. Safelite Auto Glass (windshield installation) switched from hourly wages to per-windshield piece rates over 19 months, giving Lazear a rare natural experiment with rich individual-level data. Finding: **44% average productivity gain**. Lazear decomposes the gain into two channels — **incentive effect** (workers work harder) and **selection effect** (better workers stay, worse workers leave) — and shows both contribute roughly equally. This decomposition became the field-standard empirical framework for evaluating any performance-pay initiative.

## Setup

- Safelite installs auto windshields. Job is (i) discrete and countable, (ii) individually assignable, (iii) quality easily monitored (leaks reported by customers), (iv) individual output.
- **Pre-switch**: hourly wage. Workers paid for time, not output.
- **Post-switch**: piece rate per installed windshield, with guaranteed minimum hourly rate.
- **Rollout**: staggered across ~4,000 workers over 19 months, giving within-worker before/after comparisons and cross-worker DiD.
- **Data**: rich individual-level panel — pre-hire test scores, individual output, tenure, wages.

## Identification

### Step 1 — within-worker incentive effect
Compare same worker $i$'s productivity before vs. after the switch (worker fixed effects absorb ability):
$$\text{Incentive effect} = \bar y_i^{\text{post}} - \bar y_i^{\text{pre}}.$$

### Step 2 — selection effect
Compare worker $i$'s pre-hire test scores by pre- vs. post-switch cohort. Selection effect = ability distribution of hires and stayers changes when workers' expected rewards shift.

### Step 3 — decomposition
Total productivity gain = incentive effect + selection effect. Both estimated separately.

## Results & Contribution

### Main empirical findings

1. **44% average productivity gain** for workers switched from hourly to piece rate.
2. **Roughly half from incentive effect** (same worker works harder).
3. **Roughly half from selection effect**:
   - High-productivity workers stayed and gained.
   - Low-productivity workers quit or were displaced.
   - New hires under piece-rate regime are of higher average ability than under hourly.

### Sorting channel elevated as important as incentive channel

Prior empirical work (mostly on incentive effects only) may have understated the productivity gain from performance pay by ~50%. Lazear's decomposition became field-standard.

### Boundary conditions — when piece rates work

Safelite worked because:
- **Output measurable** (installed windshield or not — binary, countable, homogeneous).
- **Quality clear** (leak → return, worker fixes on own time, at zero pay).
- **Individual production** (one worker, one car, one windshield — no cooperation externalities).
- **Task homogeneous** (all windshields roughly equal difficulty).

When these conditions fail, piece rates encounter the F1–F7 failure modes documented elsewhere in the notes.

### Contribution to the literature

1. **Field-standard empirical benchmark**. Every subsequent empirical study of PBP compares its magnitude to Lazear's 44%.
2. **Selection channel elevated** to equal importance with incentive effect.
3. **Motivated the ABM calibration**. Quindi's ABM targets the Lazear (2000) 44% total gain and ~50% sorting share as an over-identification test.
4. **Empirical foundation for tournament theory** (LR 1981) as well — piece rates and tournaments both work when the output is measurable and cooperation externalities are absent.
5. **Practical implication for firm design**. Piece rates dominate hourly pay when (i) output measurable, (ii) quality clear, (iii) individual production.
6. **Related empirical work.**
   - Paarsch–Shearer 1999, 2000: tree-planters in Canada; ~20% gain.
   - Bandiera–Barankay–Rasul 2005: UK fruit farm; social preferences REDUCE piece-rate effectiveness with peers as friends.
   - Copeland–Monnet 2009: postal workers; ~30% gain.
   - Larkin 2014: software salespeople; gaming and sandbagging under piece rates.
7. **Failure mode counter-examples**: Freeman–Kleiner 2005 (garment plant with team-pay switch); Hamilton–Nickerson–Owan 2003 (team pay outperforms individual pay in same industry).

→ Anchor: **Incentives Theory Core**

---

## Supplementary notes

**Ref.** Lazear, E. P. (2000). Performance pay and productivity. *American Economic Review*, 90(5), 1346–1361.

---

## Intro

Empirical benchmark for the **linear-contract payoff** in the field. Safelite Auto Glass switched from hourly wages to per-windshield piece rates over 19 months; rich individual-level panel data.

## Findings

- **44% average productivity gain** for workers switched from hourly to piece rate.
- Decomposition:
  - **Incentive effect** (same worker works harder): ~half.
  - **Selection effect** (better workers stay, worse leave): ~half.

## Position (empirical evidence under ②)

Yellow empirical card — supports the HM 1987 mechanism. Boundary conditions: works when (i) output measurable, (ii) quality clear, (iii) individual production.

## Contribution

Every subsequent empirical study of PBP compares its magnitude to Lazear's 44%.

---

## Contract-family view (A1 Piece Rate)

### How this modifies the base model

Layer output-contingent slope on top of $w_0$:
$$w_i = \alpha + \beta\, s_i, \quad s_i = g(e_i) + \varepsilon_i$$

Worker's problem (CARA-Gaussian):
$$\max_{e_i}\; \alpha + \beta g(e_i) - c(e_i) - \tfrac{1}{2}\rho\beta^2\sigma^2$$

FOC: $\beta\, g'(e_i^{*}) = c'(e_i^{*}) \Rightarrow e_i^{*} > 0$.

Optimal slope (Holmström–Milgrom 1987):
$$\beta^{*} = \frac{1}{1 + \rho\,\sigma^2\, k/g'^{\,2}}$$

Efficiency loss vs first-best: $\Delta = \tfrac{1}{2}\rho\sigma^2(\beta^{*})^2$.

---

**Signal**: individual measured output.

**Solves**
- Connects worker utility to firm output.
- Strong effort incentive.
- Sorts high-productivity types into the firm (Safelite: ~half the 44% gain is sorting).

**Breaks**
- Measurement error → risk transfer.
- Multitasking (Holmström–Milgrom 1991).
- Ratchet (Gibbons 1987).
- Goodhart / bunching.
- Cooperation collapse (Hamilton–Nickerson–Owan 2003).

**Use when**: output perfectly measurable, quality clearly enforceable, production individual (Safelite is the textbook case).

---

### References

- **Lazear, E. (2000)**. Performance pay and productivity. *AER*, 90(5), 1346–1361 (Safelite study, 44% productivity gain).
- **Holmström, B. & Milgrom, P. (1987)**. Aggregation and linearity in the provision of intertemporal incentives. *Econometrica*, 55(2), 303–328 (optimal linear contract).
- **Holmström, B. (1979)**. Moral hazard and observability. *Bell JE*, 10, 74–91 (canonical PA setup).
- **Grossman, S. & Hart, O. (1983)**. An analysis of the principal-agent problem. *Econometrica*, 51(1), 7–45.
- **Mirrlees, J. (1975)**. The theory of moral hazard and unobservable behaviour. Working paper (later 1999 REStud).
- **Ross, S. (1973)**. The economic theory of agency: the principal's problem. *AER Papers & Proceedings*, 63(2), 134–139.

---

## Failure-mode view (F7 Safelite preconditions)

**Three conditions that made Safelite work**

1. **Output perfectly measurable**: install-a-windshield-or-not; discrete, countable, homogeneous.
2. **Quality standard clear**: any leak/failure → worker returns to fix, unpaid, on own time. Solves the quality-quantity multitasking problem via ex-post penalty.
3. **Production individual**: no cooperation externalities to destroy. One worker, one car, one windshield.

**Implication for Quindi.AI**: violates #3 (cooperation matters) and possibly #1 (multi-dim AI-assisted output). Price cooperation, don't rely on a single scalar throughput.

---

### References

- **Lazear, E. (2000)**. Performance pay and productivity. *AER*, 90(5), 1346–1361 (Safelite study — the original documentation of the preconditions).
- **Paarsch, H. & Shearer, B. (1999)**. The response of worker effort to piece rates: evidence from the British Columbia tree-planting industry. *JHR*, 34(4), 643–667 (another individual, measurable, quality-easy-to-monitor setting).
- **Shearer, B. (2004)**. Piece rates, fixed wages and incentives: evidence from a field experiment. *REStud*, 71(2), 513–534.
- **Bandiera, O., Barankay, I. & Rasul, I. (2005)**. Social preferences and the response to incentives. *QJE*, 120(3), 917–962 (breakdown when preconditions fail).

nodes.title: P·Bloom–Van Reenen (2013) — Management Empirics
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Bloom, N., Sadun, R. & Van Reenen, J. (2013). Management as a technology? Manuscript / *NBER WP 22327* (2016); see also earlier Bloom–Van Reenen (2007) *QJE* 122(4), 1351–1408 for methodology and Bloom & Van Reenen (2010) *JEP* 24(1) survey.

## Intro

Foundational empirical work measuring **management practices** (including target-setting, performance monitoring, incentive design) across ~10,000+ firms in ~30 countries via a standardized interview instrument.

## Contribution

- **Better management practices raise productivity ~17%** on average.
- Best-managed firms have both **measurement discipline** (Holmström-1979-style informative signals) and **explicit incentive design** (HM-1987-style linear contracts on those signals).
- Poor management ≈ poor measurement ≈ effectively $\sigma^2$ high.

## Position (empirical evidence under ②)

Yellow empirical card — supports the claim that **better information + explicit incentive design** raises productivity across a very broad set of industries and countries. Complements Lazear 2000 (single firm, clean setting) with cross-country/cross-industry breadth.

nodes.title: ③ PROBLEM · Noise Remains
nodes.content:
# ③ Even with the optimal contract, noise remains

Even under HM 1987 optimal $\beta^*$, three residual problems persist:

**a) Idiosyncratic shocks:** individual output $y$ still contains noise beyond effort. The risk premium $\rho\sigma^2\beta^{*2}/2$ the firm pays scales with $\sigma^2$. When $\sigma^2$ is large, the risk premium becomes prohibitive and $\beta^*$ collapses toward 0.

**b) Multi-tasking (Holmström–Milgrom 1991):** if effort has multiple dimensions and only one is measured, the linear contract distorts effort toward the measured dimension — the worker "games" the metric.

**c) Ratchet effect (Gibbons 1987):** if the firm uses today's output to set tomorrow's target, the worker rationally hides productivity to keep future targets low.

## What's needed next

We need a contract that:
- Filters out **common shocks** (i.e. shocks correlated across agents that individual noise-based contracts can't remove).
- Doesn't require intertemporal quota-updating (avoids ratchet).
- Doesn't push all effort onto one measured dimension (avoids multitasking distortion).

The answer is to switch from a CARDINAL signal to an ORDINAL one — **rank the agents against each other**. → **Green ④** (tournaments).

nodes.title: P·Holmström–Milgrom (1991) — Multitasking
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Holmström, B. & Milgrom, P. (1991). Multitask principal-agent analyses: incentive contracts, asset ownership, job design. *JLEO*, 7(Special), 24–52.

## Contribution
**Multitasking** extension.

## Idea
Agent chooses effort vector $\mathbf{e}$; multiple signals $\mathbf{s}$ with noise covariance $\Sigma$; incentive weights $\boldsymbol\beta$.

## Result
$$\boldsymbol\beta^* = (I + \rho C \Sigma)^{-1} \mathbf{g}'$$
If one task cannot be measured ($\beta_j = 0$), agent sets $e_j = 0$; firm must **dampen ALL** $\beta_k$ to preserve balance.

## Impact
**F2 multitasking**. Direct foundation for our Quindi Optimal formula.

→ Anchor: **Incentives Theory Core**

---

## Supplementary notes

**Ref.** Holmström, B. & Milgrom, P. (1991). Multitask principal-agent analyses: Incentive contracts, asset ownership, and job design. *Journal of Law, Economics, & Organization*, 7 (Special Issue), 24–52.

---

## Intro

Extends HM 1987 to the case where the agent chooses effort across **multiple dimensions** and only some are contractible.

## Contribution

- If effort has multiple dimensions and only one is measured, the linear contract **crowds out** the unmeasured dimension.
- **The optimal $\beta$ on the measured dimension is LOW** — sometimes zero — to avoid distortion.
- Explains why teacher pay isn't strongly tied to test scores (would crowd out un-tested learning), why sales commissions can hurt customer service, why coding productivity metrics may hurt code quality.

## Position

Red **③** — a residual problem after HM 1987's linear contract. Also implicitly a **solution constraint**: when multi-tasking matters, the linear contract needs to be less aggressive.

## Empirical support

- Asch (1990) military recruiters.
- Larkin (2014) software salespeople gaming quota timing.
- Baker (1992) formalizes the multi-task distortion.

---

## Failure-mode view (F2 Multitasking)

**Problem**

If you reward one task among several, workers crowd out the un-rewarded tasks.

**Evidence**
- Asch (1990), Larkin (2014): piece rates on tasks A, B, C → worker picks only the mispriced (arbitrage) one.
- If firm tracks 3 tasks, worker finds the highest-marginal-return one and dumps the rest.

**Why**
Worker's cost of effort is convex; marginal reward differs across tasks. Optimal worker response is a corner solution unless firm equalizes marginal incentives across ALL relevant dimensions.

**Which alternatives address it**
- A3 Fixed wage (no metric to game)
- A4 Team pay (broader signal)
- A6 Career concerns (market prices overall ability)
- A7 Subjective (rewards all dimensions)
- A8 Ownership (aligned to firm value)

---

### References

- **Holmström, B. & Milgrom, P. (1991)**. Multitask principal–agent analyses: incentive contracts, asset ownership, and job design. *JLEO*, 7(Special), 24–52.
- **Baker, G. (1992)**. Incentive contracts and performance measurement. *JPE*, 100(3), 598–614.
- **Asch, B. (1990)**. Do incentives matter? The case of Navy recruiters. *ILR Review*, 43(3), 89-S–106-S.
- **Larkin, I. (2014)**. The cost of high-powered incentives: employee gaming in enterprise software sales. *Journal of Labor Economics*, 32(2), 199–227.
- **Feltham, G. & Xie, J. (1994)**. Performance measure congruity and diversity in multi-task principal/agent relations. *Accounting Review*, 69(3), 429–453.

nodes.title: P·Larkin (2014) — Empirical Gaming
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Larkin, I. (2014). The cost of high-powered incentives: Employee gaming in enterprise software sales. *Journal of Labor Economics*, 32(2), 199–227.

---

## Intro

Empirical evidence for **multi-tasking + ratchet gaming**. Studies enterprise software salespeople paid nonlinear commissions tied to quarterly quotas.

## Findings

- Salespeople **sandbag** large deals — delay them across quarter-ends to smooth commission — instead of closing them optimally for the firm.
- Sandbagging costs the firm ~6-8% of realized revenue.
- Behaviour rationally responds to nonlinear commission schedule — worker strategically shifts revenue across periods to maximize personal payoff.

## Position

Yellow **③** — empirical evidence of the multi-tasking/ratchet failure mode of piece-rate/commission contracts.

nodes.title: ④ SOLUTION · Tournaments (Rank-Order)
nodes.content:
# ④ Tournaments — pay by RANK, not by cardinal output

**Filter common shocks by comparing agents against each other.**

Lazear & Rosen (1981) show that with $N$ agents, output $y_i = e_i + \varepsilon_i$, and prizes $w_H, w_L$:
$$e^* = \frac{\Delta \cdot g \cdot f_\varepsilon(0)}{k}, \quad \Delta = w_H - w_L$$

Under risk-neutrality, choosing $\Delta^* = 1/f_\varepsilon(0)$ implements **first-best effort exactly**.

## Why tournaments solve ③

- **Common noise cancels.** If $y_i = e_i + \eta + \varepsilon_i$ with $\eta$ shared, ranks depend only on $\varepsilon_i - \varepsilon_j$; $\eta$ drops out (Nalebuff–Stiglitz 1983 sufficient-statistic argument in ordinal form).
- **No cardinal metric to game** for multi-tasking distortion (though rank creates new gaming — see phase ⑤).
- **No own-history ratchet** — the target is set by peer performance, not own past.

## Empirical evidence (yellow, below)

- **Ehrenberg–Bognanno 1990**: PGA golf, prize spread → final-round score (canonical natural experiment).
- **Casas-Arce & Martínez-Jerez 2009**: sales tournaments — inverted-U effort in interim distance.
- **Kolstad 2013**: surgeon report cards — tournament-shaped public ranking → 10% risk-adjusted mortality reduction.

## What's needed next

Tournaments create THEIR OWN failure modes:
- **Sabotage** (Lazear 1989 — pay equality and industrial politics).
- **Bunching / Goodhart** (Oyer 1998 — salespeople bunch deals around quarter-ends).
- **Cooperation collapse** (Hamilton–Nickerson–Owan 2003 — teams outperform tournaments in some settings).
- **Fairness collapse** in social settings (Bandiera–Barankay–Rasul 2005).

→ **Red ⑤**.

nodes.title: P·Nalebuff–Stiglitz (1983) — Common-Noise Filtering
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Nalebuff, B. J. & Stiglitz, J. E. (1983). Prizes and incentives: Towards a general theory of compensation and competition. *Bell Journal of Economics*, 14(1), 21–43.

---

## Intro

Formalizes the **genuine advantage of tournaments over linear contracts**: ordinal ranks are the **sufficient statistic for effort** when common shocks are present.

## Contribution

- If $y_i = e_i + \eta + \varepsilon_i$ with $\eta$ shared, ranks depend only on $\varepsilon_i - \varepsilon_j$; $\eta$ drops out.
- **Whenever $\text{Var}(\eta) > 0$, tournaments strictly Pareto-dominate linear contracts** on informativeness alone.
- Provides the theoretical basis for why competitive relative-performance evaluation is a robust design in industries with heavy common shocks (industry-wide demand, weather, technology).

## Position

Green **④** — theoretical strengthening of LR 1981.

nodes.title: ⑤ PROBLEM · Sabotage · Goodhart · Cooperation Collapse
nodes.content:
# ⑤ Tournaments create their own failure modes

**Rank pay is not a free lunch.** Once you make agents compete against each other:

**a) Sabotage (Lazear 1989):** each agent has an incentive to *lower* opponents' output. When effort and sabotage are close substitutes, tournament designs must **compress pay** to reduce sabotage incentives — which cuts the effort incentive too.

**b) Bunching / Goodhart (Oyer 1998):** when the pay schedule has kinks at quarter-ends / year-ends, agents strategically shift output across the kink. "What is measured gets manipulated."

**c) Cooperation collapse (Hamilton–Nickerson–Owan 2003; Bandiera–Barankay–Rasul 2005):** under piece rates / tournaments, agents stop helping each other. In the BBR 2005 UK fruit farm, switching FROM relative TO piece rates raised productivity 50% because workers no longer had to weigh peer welfare.

**d) Late-round distortions (Genakos–Pagliero 2012):** contestants who are ahead avoid risk; contestants who are behind take reckless risks.

## What's needed next

Contracts that:
- Reward the group, not individuals (so cooperation is a private good, not a public one).
- Use subjective evaluation to catch dimensions no metric captures.
- Rely on peer pressure — the team polices itself.

→ **Green ⑥** — team pay, subjective evaluation, peer pressure.

nodes.title: P·Lazear (1989) — Pay Equality & Sabotage
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Lazear, E. P. (1989). Pay equality and industrial politics. *Journal of Political Economy*, 97(3), 561–580.

---

## Intro

Formalizes the **sabotage** cost of tournaments.

## Argument

- If workers can both increase own output AND decrease others' output, high-powered rank pay incentivizes both.
- Optimal pay design **compresses** the prize spread — sacrificing effort incentive to reduce sabotage incentive.
- Explains observed **within-firm pay compression** relative to what LR 1981's model would predict.

## Position

Red **⑤** — a fundamental problem introduced by tournaments. Motivates the shift to team pay + subjective evaluation.

nodes.title: P·Oyer (1998) — Bunching / Goodhart
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Oyer, P. (1998). Fiscal year ends and nonlinear incentive contracts: The effect on business seasonality. *Quarterly Journal of Economics*, 113(1), 149–185.

---

## Intro

Empirical demonstration of **Goodhart-style bunching** under nonlinear commission schedules.

## Findings

- Firm-level data shows revenue **spikes before fiscal year-ends** and troughs after — the pattern's magnitude matches the size of the year-end bonus discontinuity.
- Salespeople strategically shift deal-close timing across fiscal boundaries to trigger higher commission tiers.
- Effect not driven by real demand seasonality — it's the pay schedule that produces the timing pattern.

## Contribution

- **First large-N empirical proof of the Goodhart pathology** in incentive contracts.
- Establishes that any kink or threshold in the pay schedule invites strategic timing.

## Position

Red **⑤** — bunching as a Goodhart problem created by tournaments / nonlinear commissions.

---

## Failure-mode view (F6 Goodhart / Bunching)

**Evidence**
- Oyer (1998): salespeople bunch deals before fiscal year-end.
- Larkin (2014): software sales *sandbag* large deals to avoid ratcheting next quarter.
- Camerer–Farber–Falk: taxi drivers, bike messengers stop at daily income target (backward-bending supply from loss aversion).

**Mechanism**
Any quota threshold creates a kink where marginal piece rate drops to zero (or turns negative via ratchet). Workers bunch AT the threshold — never above.

> "When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure."

**Which alternatives address it**
- A3 Fixed wage (no threshold)
- A5 Deferred comp (long horizon smooths bunching)
- A6 Career concerns (continuous market pricing)
- A7 Subjective (no bright-line target)
- A8 Ownership (long-horizon claim)

---

### References

- **Goodhart, C. (1975)**. Problems of monetary management: the U.K. experience. Papers in Monetary Economics, Reserve Bank of Australia (origin of Goodhart's Law).
- **Oyer, P. (1998)**. Fiscal year ends and non-linear incentive contracts. *QJE*, 113(1), 149–185.
- **Larkin, I. (2014)**. The cost of high-powered incentives: employee gaming in enterprise software sales. *Journal of Labor Economics*, 32(2), 199–227.
- **Camerer, C., Babcock, L., Loewenstein, G. & Thaler, R. (1997)**. Labor supply of New York City cab drivers: one day at a time. *QJE*, 112(2), 407–441.
- **Farber, H. (2015)**. Why you can't find a taxi in the rain and other labor supply lessons from cab drivers. *QJE*, 130(4), 1975–2026.
- **Chevalier, J. & Ellison, G. (1997)**. Risk taking by mutual funds as a response to incentives. *JPE*, 105(6), 1167–1200 (kink-driven behavior).

nodes.title: ⑥ SOLUTION · Team Pay · Subjective Eval · Peer Pressure
nodes.content:
# ⑥ Team pay, subjective evaluation, peer pressure

**Move from individual competition to team incentives and social monitoring.**

Three complementary mechanisms:

**a) Team pay + peer pressure (Kandel–Lazear 1992):** pay the team on shared output. In small self-selected teams, peer pressure adds a psychic cost $\psi$ to shirking:
$$c'(e^*) = g/N - \psi_1(e^*, \bar e_{-i})$$

Peer pressure > free-rider dilution → team pay dominates individual pay.

**b) Subjective evaluation (Baker–Gibbons–Murphy 1994; MacLeod 2003):** supervisor discretion catches dimensions no metric captures. Credibility requires the firm to bear a reputation cost from reneging on discretionary bonuses:
$$b \leq \delta \cdot V^{\text{future}}_{\text{firm}}$$

**c) Relational contracts (Baker–Gibbons–Murphy 2002; Levin 2003):** long-term implicit contracts self-enforced by future rents.

## Empirical evidence (yellow, below)

- **BBR 2013** (UK fruit farm follow-up): team pay + endogenous team formation → +10% productivity — REVERSING the Holmström 1982 free-rider prediction.
- **HNO 2003** (garment plant, replayed here): team pay outperforms individual pay when workers self-select teammates.
- **Frederiksen–Halliday–Koch and successors**: subjective performance ratings correlate with wage growth in field data.

## The two-sided BBR insight

The **same social ties** are a TAX under tournaments (BBR 2005) and a SUBSIDY under team pay (BBR 2013). Contract structure determines the sign. This is the empirical smoking gun for why phase ⑥ is the right solution to phase ⑤.

## Not all problems solved

- **Team pay** requires self-selection into small teams to work (Encinosa–Gaynor–Rebitzer 2007: fails in medical practices with imposed teams).
- **Subjective eval** requires the firm to have future rents credible enough to enforce truthful reporting.
- **Peer pressure** collapses in large teams where monitoring is impossible.

The presentation ends here on an honest note: **there is no universal solution to the agency problem.** Contract design is a cascade of trade-offs, and information technology (Quindi, phase ②) is a substrate that improves the terms of every trade in the cascade.

nodes.title: P·Baker–Gibbons–Murphy (2002) — Relational Theory of Firm
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Baker, G., Gibbons, R. & Murphy, K. J. (2002). Relational contracts and the theory of the firm. *Quarterly Journal of Economics*, 117(1), 39–84.

---

## Intro

Extends the BGM 1994 relational-bonus mechanism into a **theory of the firm**. Answers: what activities should be organized within a firm (with implicit contracts) vs across firms (with explicit contracts)?

## Contribution

- **Firm boundaries** = boundary of the relational contract's enforceability. Activities where relational contracts are more valuable stay inside the firm.
