## Optimal Quindi Reward Formula

# Optimal Quindi Reward Formula

## Umbrella frame (Holmström–Milgrom 1987)

> Under CARA + Gaussian noise, the optimal linear contract is $w = \alpha + \beta \cdot s$, where $s$ is a **signal vector**. Piece rates = a specific $(\beta, s)$; tournaments = ranking-based $s$; profit share = team $s$. The design choice is **what signal $s$** you contract on and **whose $s$** (self, peer, team, firm).

## Signal vector for Quindi

Four signals, each targeting a distinct failure family:

| # | Signal | Definition | Whose | Fixes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $s_3$ | Peer-relative combined index (quantity + quality) | $[q_i - \bar q_{\text{peers}}] + \lambda [Q_i - \bar Q_{\text{peers}}]$ | Self vs peers | **F1**, **F2**, **F3** |
| $s_4$ | Cooperation signal | mentoring hits, help-given, knowledge-share flags | Self + peer-reported | **F5**, **F7** |
| $s_5$ | Team output | small-team KPI ($N \approx 5$) | Team | **F5**, **F7** |
| $s_6$ | Subjective manager rating | manager's assessment | Manager | **F1**, **F2**, **F6** |

Definitions:
- $q_i$ = individual throughput (calls closed, tickets resolved),
- $Q_i$ = individual quality (CSAT, error rate, rework),
- $\bar q_{\text{peers}}, \bar Q_{\text{peers}}$ = peer-group means,
- $\lambda > 0$ = relative price of quality vs quantity.

## Contract

$$\boxed{\; w_i \;=\; \alpha \;+\; \beta_3\, s_{3}(i) \;+\; \beta_4\, s_{4}(i) \;+\; \beta_5\, s_{5} \;+\; \beta_6\, s_{6}(i) \;}$$

Unpacked:

$$
w_i \;=\; \underbrace{\alpha}_{\text{floor (F4)}} + \underbrace{\beta_3 \big[(q_i - \bar q_{\text{peers}}) + \lambda (Q_i - \bar Q_{\text{peers}})\big]}_{\text{peer-relative Q+Q, F1/F2/F3}} + \underbrace{\beta_4\, s_{4}(i)}_{\text{cooperation, F5}} + \underbrace{\beta_5\, s_{5}}_{\text{team share, F5/F7}} + \underbrace{\beta_6\, s_{6}(i)}_{\text{subjective, F1/F2/F6}}
$$

## Optimal weight vector $\boldsymbol{\beta}^{*}$

From Holmström–Milgrom (1991) multitasking:

$$\boxed{\; \boldsymbol{\beta}^{*} \;=\; \big(I + \rho\, C\, \Sigma\big)^{-1}\, \mathbf{g}' \;}$$

where $\boldsymbol{\beta} = (\beta_3, \beta_4, \beta_5, \beta_6)^\top$ and
- $\mathbf{g}' = (\partial V / \partial e_j)_{j\in\{3,4,5,6\}}$ — marginal firm value of effort on each dim,
- $C$ — effort-cost Hessian ($4 \times 4$),
- $\Sigma$ — noise covariance of $(s_3, s_4, s_5, s_6)$,
- $\rho$ — CARA risk aversion of workforce.

**Reading it**:
- $\Sigma_{jj} \uparrow$ (noisier signal) $\Rightarrow \beta_j^{*} \downarrow$: don't pay heavily on noisy signals.
- Off-diagonal $\Sigma_{jk} > 0$ (correlated) $\Rightarrow$ down-weight the noisier of the pair.
- $\rho \uparrow$ (risk-averse) $\Rightarrow$ all $\beta_j^{*} \downarrow$: shift toward fixed pay $\alpha$.

**Balance condition** (no dimension arbitrable):

$$\frac{\beta_j^{*}}{\beta_k^{*}} \;=\; \frac{g_j' / (1 + \rho\,\sigma_j^2\, k_j / g_j'^{\,2})}{g_k' / (1 + \rho\,\sigma_k^2\, k_k / g_k'^{\,2})}$$

## Optimal $\lambda^{*}$

Set $\lambda$ so quantity and quality generate equal marginal firm value:

$$\lambda^{*} \;=\; \frac{\partial V / \partial Q}{\partial V / \partial q}$$

## Estimating parameters from Quindi data

- **$\sigma_j^2$** — residual variance of $s_j$ after netting worker fixed effects.
- **$\rho$** — risk-preference survey OR back out via WTA in current pay.
- **$k_j = c_{jj}''$** — labor-supply elasticity: within-worker effort response to bonus variation.
- **$g_j'$** — firm-level regression $V = \sum_j g_j'\, s_j + \varepsilon$.

With $(\rho, \Sigma, C, \mathbf{g}', \lambda)$ estimated, $\boldsymbol\beta^{*}$ is a closed-form matrix computation.

## What this contract accomplishes

| Failure | Fixed via |
|---|---|
| **F1** measurement | $s_3$ peer-relative (common shock cancelled) + $s_6$ subjective correction |
| **F2** multitasking | Balanced $\boldsymbol\beta$ across all 4 dims, incl. $\lambda$ in $s_3$ |
| **F3** ratchet | $s_3$ peer-indexed, not history-indexed |
| **F4** risk transfer | Floor $\alpha$ + HM-optimal $\|\boldsymbol\beta\|$ |
| **F5**, **F7** cooperation | $s_4$ + $s_5$ directly price the externality (offset the peer-relative sabotage risk of $s_3$) |
| **F6** Goodhart | Multi-dim + subjective override — no single kink to game |
| **A9** selection | Structure attracts cooperative, quality-oriented types ex-ante |

## Implication for the ATE study

Use the composite outcome

$$R_i \;=\; \boldsymbol\beta^{*\top}\, \mathbf{s}_i \;=\; \beta_3^{*} s_{3}(i) + \beta_4^{*} s_{4}(i) + \beta_5^{*} s_{5} + \beta_6^{*} s_{6}(i)$$

$$\hat\tau \;=\; \bar R_{T=1} - \bar R_{T=0}$$

$\hat\tau$ is (i) invariant to intra-worker task reallocation, (ii) cooperation-aware (via $s_4, s_5$), (iii) noise-optimal (via $\Sigma$-weighting), (iv) filters common shocks (via $s_3$'s peer-relative form).

**Cautions**
- **Peer group definition**: if AI treatment is uneven across peers, $s_3$ contaminates. Fix: define peer group at untreated baseline OR use saturation design.
- **SUTVA / spillovers**: $s_5$ team component embeds treatment spillover — use saturation design to identify direct vs spillover effects.

## Bottom line

Four signals $(s_3, s_4, s_5, s_6)$, four weights $(\beta_3, \beta_4, \beta_5, \beta_6)$, plus $\alpha$ and $\lambda$. $R_i = \boldsymbol\beta^{*\top}\mathbf{s}_i$ is Quindi's evaluation index AND the outcome variable of the ATE study.

---

- **Holmström, B. & Milgrom, P. (1991)**. Multitask principal–agent analyses. *JLEO*, 7(Special), 24–52 (matrix formula).
- **Baker, G. (1992)**. Incentive contracts and performance measurement. *JPE*, 100(3), 598–614 (signal-selection theory).

# MACRO cluster

**Which ABM papers extended Bergmann 1974 to model whole national/regional economies with millions of agents.**

The three papers below are parallel contributions to macro-ABM, each adding a distinct mechanism to Bergmann's founding architecture:

- **K+S (Dosi–Fagiolo–Roventini 2010)** — adds Schumpeterian innovation + selection dynamics. Bridges Nelson-Winter evolutionary theory with Keynesian demand.
- **EURACE (Dawid et al. 2012)** — scales up 50× to 50,000+ agents. Adds management-science decision rules (Basel banking, Taylor-rule central bank).
- **CATS (Delli Gatti et al. 2011)** — adds credit-network topology and financial fragility (Minsky-style endogenous crises).

## Common thread

All three build on Bergmann's 12-step-per-period, stock-flow-consistent, distributed-decision-rule architecture. Where they differ is which macro-relevant mechanism they emphasise.

# FIRM cluster

**Which ABM papers use Bergmann's bottom-up simulation logic to model organisations rather than whole economies.**

Two distinct lineages:

**Lineage 1 — NK-landscape organisational simulation:**
- **Levinthal 1997** — imports Kauffman's NK model from evolutionary biology to explain persistent firm heterogeneity.
- **Rivkin–Siggelkow 2003** — adds a 3-tier hierarchy (workers × middle managers × top) to Levinthal's single-tier NK model.

**Lineage 2 — Endogenous firm dynamics:**
- **Axtell 2001** — firms are NOT primitives. Firms EMERGE from workers' effort + team-formation choices. Reproduces Zipf firm-size law.
- **Axtell 2018** — scales up to 100k+ agents with full labour-market clearing.

Both lineages descend from Bergmann's bottom-up logic but apply it at different scales.

nodes.title: ▼ LABOR cluster · labour-market ABM
nodes.content:
# LABOR cluster

**Which ABM papers apply Bergmann's methodology specifically to labour-market frictions, wage-setting, and unemployment.**

Rooted at **Fagiolo–Dosi–Gabriele 2004** — the first labour-market ABM where wage-setting RULES THEMSELVES evolve via replicator dynamics (population-level evolution, not just agent-level learning).

Three lineages descending from FDG:
- **Discrete-choice lineage** (Neugart 2008 → Martin–Neugart 2009): integrates McFadden logit choices with empirically calibrable coefficients from German micro-data.
- **Reinforcement-learning lineage** (Richiardi 2006 → Gemkow–Neugart 2011): temporal-difference and Q-learning for adaptive agents.
- **Fixed-heuristic lineage** (Boudreau 2010 → Neugart–Richiardi 2018 handbook synthesis): rank-based imitation as the field's null model, and the definitive field survey.

# ABM FOUNDATIONS

**The theoretical and methodological framework in which Bergmann's econ-ABM sits.** Parallel to the econ-ABM tree, not descended from it.

Three foundational threads:

**Evolutionary economics theory** — Nelson–Winter 1982 provides the theoretical framework (firms as bundles of routines under selection). Tesfatsion 2006 synthesises this and other ACE work in the *Handbook of Computational Economics*.

**Critique of representative-agent macro** — Kirman 1992 (Sonnenschein–Mantel–Debreu → ABM is the response). Farmer–Foley 2009 (Nature op-ed: the economy needs ABM after the 2008 crisis).

**ABM methodology / infrastructure** — Epstein–Axtell 1996 (Sugarscape — the founding book of modern ABM). Wilensky–Rand 2015 (NetLogo textbook). ML3 2022 (formal DSL semantics for continuous-time mixed-event ABMs).

nodes.title: ★ Research question
nodes.content:
At the crossroads of \textbf{Game Theory (Incentive theory)}, \textbf{Information Economics}, and \textbf{Labor Economics}.

## Frame from personnel economics (Lazear & Oyer 2007)




Quindi touches every one of the five classical dimensions:
Issue 1: Matching firms with workers. ← Further research
Issue 2:  **Organisation of work** ← lever 1.
Issue 3: **Incentives, turnover & compensation** ← lever 2.
Issue 4:  Skill development ← Further research
Issue 5:  Teamwork & worker empowerment. ← lever 2.

Quindi "extracts" information (signals) from data -> partly solves the unobservability issues generating inefficiencies and counterproductive game thoeretical responses (.... the issue in the prisoner dilemma)

Currenly I am addressing:  lever 1 and  lever 2

## The two levers

Quindi's raises productivity via two channels. Our job is to identify and estimate each one causally.


| Lever | What Quindi does | Effect channel |
|---|---|---|
| **1. Reorganisation** | Reassign each worker to their best-fit task | **Reallocation ** |
| **2. Incentives** | Apply an incentive contract $A_j$ and measure output | **Intensive margin** — same worker, same task, more effort |

These issues are linked to incomplete information: 1) in the first case you are missing some information on the "type" of the worker (productivity distribution across tasks -> conditional, stochastic markov processes ) and 2) in the second case we are missing some information on effort (extensive literature on moral hazard...). BTW: "1. Matching firms with workers" <- missing informatin on the "type" again... 



So... is **all about information** <- the greatest is the "signal" Quindi captures (through the index) the highest the efficiency gains. 


## Deliverables
1. **Evaluation dimensions**: identify the signals $\mathbf{s}$ on which to score workers (see **Quindi Optimal Reward Formula**). "WHO" does "WHAT" in the "BEST" way. 
2. **Worker ranking**: build a composite index $R_i = \boldsymbol\beta^{*\top} \mathbf{s}_i$ using Holmström–Milgrom (1991) weights.
3. **Use the ranking**:
   - Drive the *reorganisation* lever (who goes to which task) through the evaluation dimensions
   - Drive the *incentive* lever (pay contracts of the form $A_j$) through the worker ranking

## Two research questions (two papers)
- **Paper 1 (Incentive lever)**: given task assignment, how much does contract $A_j$ change worker effort and per-task output?  Note from behavioral econ: Information treatments alone may play a subtantial role. Just showing a worker its possible salary progression in the firm may generate (for free!) effort (Learning to See the World’s Opportunities: Memory, Mental Experiencing, and the Economic Lives of the Vulnerable, Ashraf et al 2024).  
- **Paper 2 (Reorganisation lever)**: given fixed contract, how much does AI-driven task reassignment raise firm output? → task-portfolio and assignment machinery. Super relevant RN: who are the winners and the losers? (HS or LS? young or old? easier salary progression for the young?)


## Two things to know before goign on from: 
1) Lazear (2000) AER ~44% productivity gain from switching Safelite Glass installers to a piece-rate contract. **You can generate value for a company just by switching the compensation scheme!** Half of the efficiency gains generated by changes in contracts are from workers self selection (issue 1), half from intensive effects
2) BUT no clear paper on the effects of reorganization! (not surprisingly)

nodes.title: P·Hansmann (1996) — Ownership of Enterprise
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Hansmann, H. (1996). *The Ownership of Enterprise*. Harvard University Press.

---

## Intro

Book-length theory of firm ownership. Standard economics treats "the firm" as investor-owned by default. Hansmann asks: why? Real economies exhibit rich variety — worker cooperatives (law firms, medical practices, kibbutzim), consumer cooperatives (credit unions, mutuals, farm supply co-ops), nonprofit hospitals, mutual insurance, franchisor-franchisee arrangements. Hansmann's answer: **ownership should be assigned to the class of stakeholders whose contribution is hardest to contract on ex-ante** — because the residual-claim structure gives the owning class incentives to invest in the relationship without needing complete contracts.

## Setup

- Firm has multiple stakeholder classes: workers, capital investors, consumers, suppliers.
- Each class contributes an input; each faces the risk that the firm will act opportunistically ex-post.
- **Cost of ownership** = decision-making costs + risk-bearing costs (the class must monitor the firm and bear residual risk).
- **Cost of contracting** = risk of opportunistic behaviour by the firm against a non-owning class.

## Derivation — the assignment principle

### Step 1 — cost trade-off

For each stakeholder class $k$, define:
$$\text{Total cost}(k) = \underbrace{\text{Cost of ownership by } k}_{\text{decision + risk}} + \underbrace{\text{Cost of contracting for other classes}}_{\text{opportunism risk absorbed by non-owners}}.$$

### Step 2 — optimal assignment

Assign ownership to the class $k^*$ that **minimizes total cost**. This is generally the class with the highest contracting cost (i.e., whose relationship-specific investment is hardest to protect via explicit contracts).

**Rule of thumb:**
- If capital contribution is hardest to contract on (assets are locked in, hostage): investor-owned firm (standard corporation).
- If labor contribution is hardest to contract on (partner-specific human capital): worker-owned firm (law firms, medical practices).
- If consumer contribution is hardest to contract on (consumers face a monopolist for essential goods): consumer cooperative (credit unions, farm supply co-ops).
- If input-supplier contribution is hardest (specialized inputs): producer cooperative (dairy co-ops, sugar refineries).
- If quality is unobservable to consumers (charity, hospitals): nonprofit form (avoids the profit motive that would tempt cheating on quality).

### Step 3 — comparative statics

- **Capital markets improve** → investor ownership becomes cheaper → drift toward corporate form (historical pattern).
- **Labor becomes homogeneous** → worker ownership becomes cheaper (monitoring easier) → cooperatives thrive.
- **Consumer information improves** → nonprofit form no longer necessary → for-profit hospitals emerge.

## Results & Contribution

1. **Unified theory of firm ownership**. Explains diversity of organizational forms with one principle: minimize total cost of ownership + contracting.
2. **Cooperatives and mutuals as rational responses**, not historical accidents. Explains why credit unions exist (banks face agency costs; consumer ownership solves it) and why they decline as banking becomes competitive.
3. **Nonprofit hospitals and universities** — where output quality is unobservable, the nonprofit form removes the profit motive to shave quality. Consistent with Newhouse 1970 and Weisbrod 1988 on the nonprofit sector.
4. **Explains capital-intensive vs. labor-intensive industries** patterns. Capital-intensive industries → investor ownership dominates. Labor-intensive skilled industries → worker cooperatives (accounting, law, consulting).
5. **Foundation for the "stakeholder theory of the firm"** in strategic management and corporate governance.
6. **Empirical follow-ups.** Kruse–Blasi 1997 on employee stock ownership plans (ESOPs); Dow 2003 on worker-owned firms; Cheney–Cruz–Peredo–Nazareno 2014 on worker cooperatives worldwide.
7. **Relation to Jensen–Meckling 1976:** JM assume investor ownership and analyze agency costs within it; Hansmann asks *why* investor ownership rather than other forms — extending the framework upstream.

→ Anchor: **Incentives Theory Core**

---

## Contract-family view (A8 Ownership / Equity)

### How this modifies the base model

Add equity share $\phi \in (0,1)$ on top of $w_0$:
$$w_i = w_0 + \phi \cdot V, \qquad V = \sum_{j=1}^N y_j$$

Marginal own-effort incentive:
$$\frac{\partial w_i}{\partial e_i} = \phi \cdot \frac{\partial V}{\partial e_i}$$

For workforce size $N$, effective incentive per worker on own task is $\phi/N$ — free-rider like team pay. But alignment with **long-run** firm value handles multi-dim + horizon simultaneously.

---

**Signal**: firm value — worker holds a residual claim (stock, options, partnership share, ESOP).

**Solves**
- Aligns effort with long-run firm value → solves multitasking (F2) and horizon jointly.
- Rewards firm-level cooperation and mentoring (F5).
- Long horizon smooths short-run bunching (F6).
- Prices cooperation externality → useful when Safelite condition #3 (individual production) fails (F7).

**Breaks**
- Free-rider grows with N (each worker owns ≈ 1/N).
- Loads undiversified risk onto workers (labor income + wealth co-move) — WORSENS F4.
- Governance costs — worker-owners may block value-creating layoffs.
- Requires liquidity / vesting to prevent early cash-out.

**Use when**: small firm, high-skill workers, long horizon, output primarily reflects team effort (early-stage startup, law/consulting partnership).

---

### References

- **Hansmann, H. (1996)**. *The Ownership of Enterprise*. Harvard University Press.
- **Kruse, D. & Blasi, J. (1997)**. Employee ownership, employee attitudes, and firm performance. In *The Human Resources Management Handbook*.
- **Jensen, M. & Meckling, W. (1976)**. Theory of the firm: managerial behavior, agency costs and ownership structure. *JFE*, 3(4), 305–360.
- **Blasi, J., Kruse, D. & Freeman, R. (2018)**. Broad-based employee stock ownership and profit sharing. *Journal of Participation and Employee Ownership*, 1(1), 38–60.
- **Oyer, P. (2004)**. Why do firms use incentives that have no incentive effects? *Journal of Finance*, 59(4), 1619–1650.

nodes.title: P·Holmström (1982) — Moral Hazard in Teams
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Holmström, B. (1982). Moral hazard in teams. *Bell Journal of Economics*, 13(2), 324–340.

---

## Intro

**Founding paper of team moral hazard.** Distinct from Holmström (1982) *Managerial Incentive Problems* (career concerns) — same year, different Bell issue. Answers: in team production where individual effort is unobservable and only aggregate output is measurable, can any budget-balanced sharing rule implement first-best?

## Setup

- $N$ team members choose effort $e_i$ at private cost $c_i(e_i)$.
- Aggregate output $y = f(e_1, ..., e_N)$ is observable; individual $e_i$ is not.
- **Budget-balanced sharing rule**: $\sum_i s_i(y) = y$ (nothing lost, nothing added).

## Free-rider theorem

Under budget balance + equal sharing, worker $i$'s FOC is:
$$\frac{1}{N} \cdot \frac{\partial y}{\partial e_i} = c_i'(e_i^*)$$

Marginal reward on own effort scales with $1/N$ — free-rider effect grows with team size. First-best requires $\partial y/\partial e_i = c_i'$, so equal sharing gives underprovision by factor $N$.

## Impossibility result

**No budget-balanced sharing rule implements first-best.** Requires a **residual claimant** (Alchian–Demsetz 1972 style) who breaks budget balance — burns output if targets are missed, redistributes surplus if targets are met.

## Contribution

- Establishes the **fundamental limit of team pay** in the absence of monitoring or peer pressure.
- Motivates every subsequent paper on team incentives:
  - **Kandel–Lazear (1992)** — peer pressure adds the missing wedge.
  - **Bandiera–Barankay–Rasul (2013)** — endogenous team formation resolves it empirically.
  - **Hamilton–Nickerson–Owan (2003)** — self-selection into teams reverses the free-rider prediction.
- Referenced in the yardstick-competition literature (Shleifer 1985) as motivation for peer-benchmarked contracts.

→ Anchor: parent to **P·Kandel–Lazear (1992)** in the Phase-6 team-pay branch.

nodes.title: P·Weitzman (1980) — The Ratchet Principle
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Weitzman, M. L. (1980). The "ratchet principle" and performance incentives. *Bell Journal of Economics*, 11(1), 302–308.

---

## Intro

**Original formal treatment of the ratchet effect** — in the Soviet-planning context. Central planner sets next period's quota based on this period's realized output. Firm rationally under-produces today to avoid tighter targets tomorrow. Weitzman formalises what Roy (1952) had documented ethnographically in US machine shops and what became the canonical dynamic-incentive puzzle.

## Setup

- Soviet enterprise with hidden productivity $\theta$.
- Planner sets quota $q_t$; enterprise chooses effort $e_t$; output $y_t = \theta e_t$ observed.
- Planner updates: $q_{t+1} = q_t + \lambda(y_t - q_t)$ — reward attainment, ratchet on excess.

## Result

Firm's optimal $e_t^*$ falls short of the static optimum: the future-quota penalty $\lambda \cdot$ (discount factor) exactly offsets today's marginal reward for extra effort. Enterprises pool at the quota — never above.

## Contribution

- **First formal model of dynamic incentive distortion.** Predates Gibbons (1987) by 7 years but was largely confined to the planning literature.
- Explains observed under-performance in centrally planned economies and quota-based sales organizations.
- **Foundation for the dynamic-mechanism-design literature** — Freixas-Guesnerie-Tirole 1985 provides the fully rational-expectations extension; Laffont-Tirole 1988 studies commitment as the solution.

→ Anchor: parent-in-lineage to **P·Gibbons (1987)** in the Phase-3 ratchet cluster.

nodes.title: P·Freixas–Guesnerie–Tirole (1985) — Ratchet Effect Formalized
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Freixas, X., Guesnerie, R. & Tirole, J. (1985). Planning under incomplete information and the ratchet effect. *Review of Economic Studies*, 52(2), 173–191.

---

## Intro

**Fully-rational-expectations formalization of the ratchet effect.** Extends Weitzman (1980) with Bayesian updating and strategic signal-jamming. The canonical theoretical statement of the ratchet problem that Gibbons (1987) then applies to the labor context.

## Setup

- Two-period model. Planner and firm both play Nash.
- Firm has private type $\theta$; observable output $y_1 = f(\theta, e_1)$; planner updates belief about $\theta$ from $y_1$.
- Period-2 quota is chosen conditional on inferred $\theta$.

## Result

- **Firms strategically pool** — high-$\theta$ firm chooses $e_1$ equal to what a low-$\theta$ firm would choose, to prevent the planner from learning $\theta$.
- **Full separation is impossible** without commitment: the planner would love to promise "I won't ratchet", but ex-post has no incentive to honour that promise, so firms don't believe it.
- **Long-term commitment** (Laffont-Tirole 1988) restores efficiency; **no commitment** produces the pooling equilibrium.

## Contribution

- **Foundation for dynamic mechanism design** with private information and adverse selection.
- Provides the game-theoretic rigor Weitzman (1980) lacked.
- Direct predecessor to **Laffont-Tirole 1988** (formal commitment solution) and **Gibbons 1987** (labour-context application).

→ Anchor: extends **P·Weitzman (1980)**, leads into **P·Gibbons (1987)** and **P·Laffont–Tirole (1988)**.

nodes.title: P·Bloom (1999) — Pay Dispersion Effects
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Bloom, M. (1999). The performance effects of pay dispersion on individuals and organizations. *Academy of Management Journal*, 42(1), 25–40.

---

## Intro

**Empirical challenge to tournament theory's steep-prize prediction.** Studies Major League Baseball teams as a natural laboratory for pay-dispersion effects on team performance. Rosen (1986) predicts steeper prize spreads → more effort → better outcomes. Bloom finds the OPPOSITE for team sports.

## Setup

- Panel of MLB teams 1985-1993.
- Within-team pay dispersion (Gini coefficient of player salaries) as key regressor.
- Team-performance outcomes: winning percentage, playoff appearances, revenue.

## Findings

- **More compressed pay structures → better team performance.**
- **Wider dispersion → worse team performance**, especially for teams where cooperation is critical (defense metrics fall more than individual offensive stats).
- Effect concentrated among lower-paid players: they under-perform when the star's salary is very high relative to theirs.

## Contribution

- **Empirical counter-example to naïve tournament theory** in team settings.
- Rationalizes observed **within-firm pay compression** documented by Baker-Jensen-Murphy 1988.
- Supports **Lazear 1989 sabotage** framework: pay dispersion incentivizes sabotage / withdrawal of cooperation.
- Motivates the **KL 1992 peer pressure** and **BBR 2013 team incentives** solutions.

## Boundary conditions

- Applies to sports and other team-cooperation settings.
- Does NOT invalidate Rosen (1986) for individual-contest settings (executive tournaments, sales contests without cooperation).

→ Anchor: sibling of **P·Rosen (1986)** — empirical evidence that qualifies tournament theory's prescription.

nodes.title: P·Jensen–Murphy (1990) — CEO Pay-Performance Sensitivity
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Jensen, M. C. & Murphy, K. J. (1990). Performance pay and top-management incentives. *Journal of Political Economy*, 98(2), 225–264.

---

## Intro

The **famous "$3.25 per $1000"** paper. Documents that CEO wealth changes only \$3.25 for every \$1,000 change in shareholder wealth — a pay-performance sensitivity of ~0.325%. Concludes observed CEO compensation cannot possibly provide the incentive alignment classical agency theory predicts.

## Setup

- Sample of ~2,000 CEOs of large US corporations, 1974-1988.
- Estimate the sensitivity of CEO wealth (salary + bonus + stock + options + dismissal probability) to changes in shareholder wealth.

## Findings

- **Median pay-performance sensitivity: $3.25 per $1,000** of shareholder wealth change.
- Decomposition:
  - Salary + bonus: ~$1.35
  - Stock ownership: ~$0.75
  - Options: ~$0.50
  - Dismissal risk: ~$0.65
- Sensitivity **declined** through the sample period (contrary to popular narrative of "increased" pay-for-performance).
- Sensitivity is HIGHER for smaller firms and DECREASES with firm size (harder to concentrate ownership in a giant firm).

## Contribution

- **Field-defining empirical benchmark** for CEO agency. Every subsequent study of executive compensation compares its sensitivity to Jensen-Murphy's $3.25.
- **Puzzle for agency theory**: if sensitivity is this low, either agency costs are trivial (unlikely) or observed compensation is a poor solution to the agency problem.
- Motivates the subsequent literature:
  - **BJM 1988 (already in the tree)** — real contracts vs theoretical predictions.
  - **Hall-Liebman 1998** — the stock-option boom of the 1990s changed the sensitivity story.
  - **Bandiera-Prat-Sadun 2020 (in the tree)** — measure CEO behaviour directly rather than inferring from pay-performance sensitivity.

→ Anchor: successor to **P·Baker–Jensen–Murphy (1988)** in the empirical CEO-agency chain.

nodes.title: ★ Reorganization Theory — Core
nodes.content:
# Reorganization Theory — Core

**Paper 2's central question.**

Given $N$ workers each with a distribution of skills $\{\alpha_{ij}\}$ across $K$ tasks, and given the firm can observe worker types, how much output does OPTIMAL REASSIGNMENT generate over the status-quo?

$$V^{*} \;=\; \max_{\mu:\, [N]\to[K]} \sum_i g(\alpha_{i,\mu(i)}) \;-\; \sum_i g(\alpha_{i,\mu_0(i)})$$

where $\mu_0$ is the status-quo assignment and $\mu$ is the reassignment enabled by type-observation.





## The three sub-questions Paper 2 answers

1. **WHY** does reassignment generate value? → Roy model + assignment theory (foundational).
2. **HOW MUCH** value in practice? → Multidimensional skill mismatch literature + FIELD EXPERIMENTS (empirical cluster + direct-interventions cluster).
3. **WHY NOW** is this feasible? → AI / IT / management-practice as type-observation technologies (enablers).

## The six literature clusters

1. **▼ Roy & Assignment theory** — theoretical foundation. Roy (1951), Heckman-Sedlacek (1985), Rosen (1982), Sattinger (1993), Garicano (2000), Costinot-Vogel (2010), Lazear (1995).

2. **▼ Skill Heterogeneity & Mismatch Value** All these papers MEASURE mismatch — none actually intervenes.

3. **▼ Field experiments ** Exploring how productivity is assigned by "who does what" 

4. **▼ Reorganization Value · pre-AI empirical estimates** — historical bounds from IT and management-practice studies: ISP 1997 (~7%), BBH 2002/BIS 2007 (15-20%), BEMMR 2013 (17%), HK 2009 (30-60% macro upper bound).

5. **▼ Task-Based framework** — context: how technology reshapes the α-matrix (ALM 2003, Acemoglu-Autor 2011, Autor 2015/2019, Acemoglu-Restrepo 2018/2022, Deming 2017).

6. **▼ Gen-AI Empirical** — modern type-observation enabler: BLR 2023, Peng 2023, Noy-Zhang 2023, Dell'Acqua 2023, Athey-Bryan-Gans 2020, Beane 2019.

## Winners / losers — heterogeneous treatment effects

Central to Paper 2's contribution:
- **High-skill vs low-skill** — compression (BLR 2023, Guvenen et al 2020) or polarization (G-RH 2006)?
- **Junior vs senior** — apprenticeship channel effects (Beane 2019).
- **Specialists vs generalists** — the α-matrix determines who wins.

nodes.title: ▼ Roy & Assignment theory · why reassignment generates value
nodes.content:
# Roy & Assignment theory · why reassignment generates value

**The theoretical foundation of Paper 2.** Explains WHY worker-task comparative advantage generates positive value from sorting.

## Three theoretical lineages

**Roy model — self-selection based on comparative advantage** (Roy 1951)
- Workers self-select into occupations where their comparative advantage is highest.
- Aggregate output strictly higher than random assignment.
- Empirical extensions: Heckman-Sedlacek (1985) structural estimation, Heckman-Honoré (1990) identification, Borjas (1987) migration application.

**Assignment models — optimal matching of heterogeneous types** (Rosen 1982, Sattinger 1993)
- Given $\theta_i$ worker type × $\sigma_j$ task complexity, optimal assignment $\sigma^*(\theta)$ under log-supermodularity gives positive assortative matching (PAM).
- Wage function determined by marginal-product-along-matching integral.
- Applied to HR / firm design by Lazear (1995) *Personnel Economics* → Lazear-Oyer (2013) handbook chapter.

**Knowledge hierarchies — technology-sensitive assignment** (Garicano 2000)
- Workers specialise in the frequency of problems they solve; hard problems escalate upward.
- Extended in Garicano-Rossi-Hansberg (2006) — technology (including AI) changes the optimal cutoffs, forcing reassignment.
- Continuous generalisation: Costinot-Vogel (2010).

## The prediction Paper 2 tests

If $\{\alpha_{ij}\}$ is not rank-invariant across tasks (i.e., some workers are relatively better at some tasks than others), then optimal reassignment generates strictly positive value $V^* > 0$. The **magnitude** depends on the dispersion of $\alpha$ within workers across tasks — quantified in the next cluster.

→ Anchor: **Reorganization Theory — Core**

nodes.title: ▼ Task-Based framework · technology reallocates tasks (enabler context)
nodes.content:
# Task-Based framework · technology reallocates tasks

**Enabler-context cluster.** Explains how technology reshapes the task landscape that assignment operates on — the WHY NOW dimension.

## What this cluster establishes

Instead of technology raising productivity of all workers equally (SBTC), the task-based view asks:
- Which SPECIFIC tasks does technology automate vs complement?
- How does the task landscape evolve, and how does wage distribution respond?

## The lineage

**Foundational** (Autor-Levy-Murnane 2003) — routine vs non-routine × cognitive vs manual taxonomy. Computers displaced routine tasks; complemented non-routine cognitive.

**Formalised** (Acemoglu-Autor 2011) — Handbook chapter with continuum-of-tasks GE model. Workers vs capital compete for tasks; wages set by market clearing.

**Autor extensions** — Autor (2015) "why still so many jobs" (Polanyi's paradox); Autor (2019) "work of the past/future" (geographic heterogeneity).

**Acemoglu-Restrepo modernization** — A&R (2018) race between man and machine (displacement vs reinstatement); A&R (2022) decomposes 50-70% of US wage inequality via task reallocation.

**Deming (2017)** — social skills as complements to non-routine cognitive: what remains valuable when tasks are re-shuffled.

## Role in Paper 2

Provides the CONTEXT for the reassignment question:
- The task landscape is itself dynamic (technology reshapes it).
- Paper 2's $\{\alpha_{ij}\}$ matrix is not static — it evolves as tasks change.
- Explains WHY the reassignment question is timely (task landscape shifting fastest since Industrial Revolution).

→ Anchor: **Reorganization Theory — Core**

nodes.title: ▼ Gen-AI Empirical · modern type-observation enabler
nodes.content:
# Gen-AI Empirical · modern type-observation enabler

**Enabler cluster.** Field experiments and RCTs measuring how generative AI actually changes worker productivity and — crucially for Paper 2 — how it enables the firm to observe $\{\alpha_{ij}\}$ at scale.

## Three families of evidence

**Customer service** (Brynjolfsson-Li-Raymond 2023) — 5,179 agents given AI assistant. **14% average productivity gain**, but **bottom-quartile +34%, top-quartile ~0%**. AI substitutes for tacit knowledge → compresses within-firm productivity distribution.

**Software engineering** (Peng et al 2023 GitHub Copilot RCT) — **55.8% faster** task completion. Junior developers gained more than seniors.

**Professional writing** (Noy-Zhang 2023, Science) — ChatGPT: 40% faster + 18% higher quality. Time shifted from drafting to editing.

**Knowledge work + "jagged frontier"** (Dell'Acqua et al 2023 BCG × GPT-4) — AI helps on tasks INSIDE its capability, hurts on tasks OUTSIDE. Skill required to filter AI output.

**Theoretical framework** (Athey-Bryan-Gans 2020) — allocation of decision authority between humans and AI. When to delegate / consult / overrule.

**Cautionary tale** (Beane 2019) — shadow learning in robotic surgery. When automation displaces the trainer role, apprenticeship breaks.

## Role in Paper 2

- Establishes that AI reveals $\{\alpha_{ij}\}$ that were previously hidden (BLR 14% gain is largely the value of NEWLY-OBSERVED types).
- Provides the current empirical benchmarks Paper 2's ABM must match.
- Winners/losers evidence: BLR compression finding directly informs Paper 2's heterogeneous-effects section.

**Direct empirical bridge to Paper 2's central question**: BLR's 14% is a lower-bound estimate of the value of type-observation-enabled reassignment in customer service. Paper 2 generalizes this to a broader class of firms with counterfactual identification.

→ Anchor: **Reorganization Theory — Core**

nodes.title: P·Rosen (1982) — Authority & Distribution of Earnings
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Rosen, S. (1982). Authority, control, and the distribution of earnings. *Bell Journal of Economics*, 13(2), 311–323.

---

## Intro

The **founding paper of talent-based hierarchical assignment.** Explains why earnings distributions have a stretched right tail: small differences in ability translate into large differences in earnings when talent operates on a larger scale via hierarchy.

## Setup

- Firm has a hierarchy with $L$ layers.
- Worker at layer $\ell$ manages workers at layer $\ell - 1$.
- Talent scales multiplicatively: a manager with talent $\theta$ multiplies each subordinate's output by $\theta$.

## Result

- Optimal assignment sorts high-$\theta$ workers into higher layers.
- Marginal returns to talent grow exponentially with layer.
- **Earnings distribution has a stretched right tail** driven purely by hierarchical assignment — not by superstar demand-side (that came later in Rosen 1981 superstars, Rosen 1986 elimination tournaments).

## Contribution

- Precursor to knowledge hierarchies (Garicano 2000).
- Complement to Rosen (1986) elimination tournaments in Paper 1.
- Assignment as a source of within-firm wage inequality — reappears in Song et al. 2019 empirical work.

→ Anchor: **Assignment theory cluster**

nodes.title: P·Sattinger (1993) — Assignment Models Survey
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Sattinger, M. (1993). Assignment models of the distribution of earnings. *Journal of Economic Literature*, 31(2), 831–880.

---

## Intro

**Field-defining survey of assignment models.** Establishes the template for how comparative advantage between heterogeneous workers and heterogeneous jobs generates earnings distributions.

## Contribution

- Provides the taxonomy of assignment models: Roy (1951) selection, Tinbergen (1956) matching, Ricardian comparative advantage, task-based extensions.
- Formalizes: worker $i$ of type $\theta_i$ matched to job $j$ of complexity $c_j$; output $f(\theta_i, c_j)$; equilibrium wage determined by market clearing.
- **Log-supermodularity** of $f$ generates positive assortative matching.
- The template for later empirical work: Costinot-Vogel (2010), Acemoglu-Autor (2011).

## Why it matters for Paper 2

If task assignment is a free parameter (as AI enables), the Sattinger framework is exactly the right lens. Reorganization = re-matching workers to tasks along comparative advantage.

→ Anchor: extends **Rosen (1982)**; template for **Costinot-Vogel (2010)**.

nodes.title: P·Garicano (2000) — Knowledge Hierarchies
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Garicano, L. (2000). Hierarchies and the organization of knowledge in production. *Journal of Political Economy*, 108(5), 874–904.

---

## Intro

One of the **most important organizational-economics papers of the last 25 years.** Explains why firms are organized as hierarchies with experts at the top: knowledge/attention is scarce, and hierarchies economize on it by referring hard problems upward.

## Setup

- Problems arrive with a distribution of complexity.
- Workers can solve any problem below their knowledge threshold $z$; refer harder problems upward.
- Higher-$z$ workers cost more to hire (higher training).
- Communication cost $h$ per referral.

## Result

- Firm chooses $L$ (number of layers) + $z_\ell$ (threshold at each layer) to minimize total cost.
- **Optimal hierarchy**: low-$z$ workers handle common problems; rare problems escalate to specialists.
- Comparative statics:
  - Cheaper communication → flatter hierarchies, more layers.
  - Cheaper problems (routine) → fewer specialists needed.

## Contribution

- **Foundation** for a large literature on knowledge hierarchies (Garicano-Rossi-Hansberg 2006, 2015).
- Explains observed layered structure of professional-services firms (consulting, law, medicine).
- **Directly relevant to Paper 2**: AI is a technology that changes the cost of solving problems at each level → reshapes the optimal hierarchy → forces reassignment.

→ Anchor: **Assignment theory cluster**; children: **G&R-H (2006)**, **Costinot-Vogel (2010)**

nodes.title: P·Garicano–Rossi-Hansberg (2006) — Org & Inequality
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Garicano, L. & Rossi-Hansberg, E. (2006). Organization and inequality in a knowledge economy. *Quarterly Journal of Economics*, 121(4), 1383–1435.

---

## Intro

Extends Garicano (2000) with **endogenous knowledge acquisition + wage distribution effects.** Answers: how does the internal organization of firms determine the wage distribution across skills?

## Setup

- Continuous distribution of worker skill.
- Firms choose hierarchy structure endogenously.
- Workers choose knowledge acquisition ex-ante.

## Result

- **Assortative matching**: high-skill workers sort into upper layers.
- Technology (ICT lowering communication cost) → higher-skill workers become more valuable, wage inequality rises.
- Explains the observed "hollowing out" of middle-skill jobs: technology reduces the value of intermediate-layer supervisors.

## Contribution

- Very close to Paper 2's framing: technology → task reallocation → wage inequality.
- **Direct prediction**: AI lowering solving-cost at low layers should REDUCE returns to low-layer workers (they're substituted) but INCREASE returns to high-layer workers (leverage grows).
- BLR (2023) finding — bottom-quartile customer service agents gain most from AI — is empirical evidence AGAINST this prediction in the customer-service context. Interesting tension for the paper.

→ Anchor: extends **Garicano (2000)**

nodes.title: P·Costinot–Vogel (2010) — Matching & Inequality
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Costinot, A. & Vogel, J. (2010). Matching and inequality in the world economy. *Journal of Political Economy*, 118(4), 747–786.

---

## Intro

**Unified assignment framework** with continuous worker types and continuous task complexities. Generalizes Sattinger (1993) and connects the assignment literature to international trade.

## Setup

- Worker skill $\theta \in [\underline\theta, \bar\theta]$; task complexity $\sigma \in [\underline\sigma, \bar\sigma]$.
- Production function $f(\theta, \sigma)$ log-supermodular → positive assortative matching.
- Continuous market clearing.

## Result

- **PAM**: unique equilibrium assignment $\sigma^*(\theta)$ increasing in $\theta$.
- **Wage function**: $w(\theta) = \int_{\underline\theta}^\theta \partial f/\partial\theta$ evaluated along the matching curve.
- Comparative statics on skill supply changes: adding low-skill workers RAISES the wages of ALL workers above them (via reallocation toward higher-complexity tasks).

## Why it matters for Paper 2

- Provides the **general theoretical apparatus** for continuous task reallocation.
- AI-enabled reassignment IS a shift in the matching function $\sigma^*(\theta)$. C-V's comparative statics give predictions about who gains and loses.

→ Anchor: extends **Sattinger (1993)** and **Garicano (2000)**

nodes.title: P·Lazear (1995) — Personnel Economics
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Lazear, E. P. (1995). *Personnel Economics.* MIT Press. Wicksell Lectures.

---

## Intro

**Founding book of "personnel economics"** as a distinct field. Applies rigorous economic theory (agency, matching, tournaments, human capital) to HR practice: hiring, promotion, job design, compensation.

## Structure

- Ch 1: The Employment Relationship (agency framework).
- Ch 2: Wage Structure (tournaments, promotions).
- Ch 3: Sorting Through Compensation.
- Ch 4: Turnover and Retirement.
- Ch 5: Payment Methods (piece rate, bonus, deferred pay).
- Ch 6: Fringe Benefits.
- Ch 7: Team Compensation.

## Contribution

- **Treats task assignment as an HR decision**, explicitly. Provides the applied bridge between assignment theory (Rosen, Sattinger) and firm-level practice.
- Field-defining textbook. Extended in Lazear-Shaw (2007) and Lazear-Oyer (2013).
- **For Paper 2**: the analytical toolkit for translating task-reassignment predictions into HR-implementable policies.

→ Anchor: extends **Sattinger (1993)**; child: **Lazear-Oyer (2013)**

nodes.title: P·Lazear–Oyer (2013) — Personnel Economics Handbook
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Lazear, E. P. & Oyer, P. (2013). Personnel economics. Chapter 12 in *Handbook of Organizational Economics* (Gibbons, R. & Roberts, J., eds.), pp. 479–519. Princeton University Press.

---

## Intro

**Handbook synthesis** of the personnel-economics literature circa 2013. The reference chapter for anyone entering the field.

## Structure

- Job design (including task assignment).
- Compensation and incentives.
- Careers and turnover.
- Team production and peer effects.
- Recruitment and selection.

## Contribution

- Consolidates 20+ years of empirical progress since Lazear (1995).
- **Positions task assignment** as a core HR lever alongside compensation.
- Emphasises comparative-advantage sorting in job design (Roy-style).
- **For Paper 2**: the definitive reference for the current state of personnel economics on task assignment.

→ Anchor: extends **Lazear (1995)**

nodes.title: P·Autor–Levy–Murnane (2003) — Skill Content of Technological Change
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Autor, D. H., Levy, F. & Murnane, R. J. (2003). The skill content of recent technological change: An empirical exploration. *Quarterly Journal of Economics*, 118(4), 1279–1333.

---

## Intro

**Founding paper of the task-based approach to labour economics.** Answers: what specifically does technology substitute for and complement?

## Framework

Tasks classified along two dimensions:
- **Routine vs non-routine** (rule-based vs judgement-based).
- **Cognitive vs manual** (thinking vs physical).

Four cells; computers substitute for **routine** tasks (both cognitive and manual) and complement **non-routine cognitive** tasks (analysis, communication).

## Empirical findings

Between 1960 and 1998:
- **Routine cognitive** task share fell 8pp.
- **Routine manual** task share fell 3pp.
- **Non-routine cognitive** task share ROSE 15pp.
- **Non-routine manual** task share unchanged.

## Contribution

- Replaces the canonical skill-biased-technical-change (SBTC) model with a task-based framework.
- **Explains wage polarization** (Autor-Katz-Kearney 2006): middle jobs (many routine tasks) hollow out; top and bottom grow.
- Foundation for Acemoglu-Autor 2011, Autor 2015, Acemoglu-Restrepo 2018.
- **For Paper 2**: gives the taxonomy for classifying which tasks AI substitutes vs complements.

→ Anchor: **Task-based cluster**; child: **Deming (2017)**

nodes.title: P·Deming (2017) — Rise of Social Skills
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Deming, D. J. (2017). The growing importance of social skills in the labor market. *Quarterly Journal of Economics*, 132(4), 1593–1640.

---

## Intro

**Extends ALM 2003** by adding *social skills* as a complement to non-routine cognitive tasks. Answers: why did the labour market keep rewarding college graduates in the 2000s despite the routine-cognitive-decline (Beaudry-Green-Sand "great reversal")?

## Empirical findings

Between 1980 and 2012:
- Jobs requiring HIGH social skills + HIGH math skills grew **24 percentage points**.
- Jobs requiring HIGH math but LOW social skills stagnated or declined.
- Social-skill returns rose sharply after 2000.

## Framework

Social skills are the technology that lets workers TRADE tasks efficiently within teams. As tasks become more specialized, coordination cost rises, and social skills become the binding scarce input.

## Contribution

- **Explains why humans still matter** in high-cognitive settings: coordination + persuasion + judgement in social contexts are hard to automate.
- Extends ALM 2003 with a THIRD dimension: routine × cognitive × social.
- **For Paper 2**: AI substitutes for the cognitive tasks; social + judgement tasks become the human comparative advantage. Predicts winners will be generalists with social skills.

→ Anchor: extends **ALM (2003)**

nodes.title: P·Acemoglu–Autor (2011) — Skills, Tasks, and Technologies
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Acemoglu, D. & Autor, D. (2011). Skills, tasks and technologies: Implications for employment and earnings. In *Handbook of Labor Economics*, Vol. 4B, pp. 1043–1171. Elsevier.

---

## Intro

**Handbook chapter formalizing the task-based framework** that ALM 2003 introduced. The theoretical apparatus underlying essentially all subsequent work on technology + wages.

## Setup

- Continuum of tasks $i \in [0, 1]$.
- Each task done by one of: high-skill labour, low-skill labour, or capital.
- Output aggregator over tasks.
- Comparative-advantage rankings determine allocation.

## Key results

- **Task allocation frontier**: cut-offs $I_L, I_H$ divide tasks among low-skill, high-skill, capital.
- Technology (falling capital cost) shifts $I_L, I_H$ right — capital captures more tasks.
- **Wages driven by task allocation**, not by aggregate factor supplies.

## Contribution

- Rigorous general-equilibrium version of ALM 2003.
- **Foundation for Acemoglu-Restrepo (2018, 2022) task-decomposition of inequality.**
- Direct precursor to Autor (2015) "still so many jobs" and Autor (2019) commuting-zone analysis.
- **For Paper 2**: canonical framework for translating "AI takes tasks" into wage-distribution predictions.

→ Anchor: extends **ALM (2003)**; child: **Autor (2015)**

nodes.title: P·Autor (2015) — Why Are There Still So Many Jobs?
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Autor, D. H. (2015). Why are there still so many jobs? The history and future of workplace automation. *Journal of Economic Perspectives*, 29(3), 3–30.

---

## Intro

Answers the popular-press worry ("robots will take all our jobs") by applying the task-based framework: automation destroys *tasks*, not necessarily jobs. New tasks and services emerge.

## Argument

- Historical pattern: automation of specific tasks → productivity gain → income effect → demand shift toward new services → new tasks created.
- **Polanyi's paradox**: many tasks require tacit knowledge that can't be codified for automation.
- Complementarity between automated tasks and human residual tasks preserves labour demand.

## Predictions

- Middle-skill jobs (heavy on routine tasks) continue to erode.
- High-skill non-routine cognitive + low-skill manual jobs relatively protected.
- **Uncertainty**: does gen-AI break Polanyi's paradox by learning tacit patterns from data?

## For Paper 2

- Establishes the "polarization" prediction. Gen-AI evidence (BLR 2023) suggests the pattern may REVERSE for cognitive tasks — reducing polarization.
- The tension between Autor (2015) and BLR (2023) is central to Paper 2's contribution.

→ Anchor: extends **Acemoglu-Autor (2011)**; child: **Autor (2019)**

nodes.title: P·Autor (2019) — Work of the Past, Work of the Future
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Autor, D. H. (2019). Work of the past, work of the future. *AEA Papers and Proceedings*, 109, 1–32. (Richard T. Ely Lecture.)

---

## Intro

**AEA presidential lecture** documenting how the collapse of middle-skill jobs varies dramatically across US commuting zones. Introduces the concept of "work of the past" (routine tasks) vs "work of the future" (non-routine social + cognitive).

## Empirical findings

- Middle-skill routine jobs disappeared roughly equally across regions.
- **Non-college workers in dense/urban zones** transitioned to non-routine service jobs (health, food service, personal care) — lower wages but stayed employed.
- **Non-college workers in less-dense zones** experienced sharp declines in employment and wages.
- **College workers** absorbed the growth in high-skill non-routine work — concentrated in dense zones.

## Contribution

- **Geographic heterogeneity** is central to understanding technology's labour-market effects.
- Explains "the geography of despair" (Case-Deaton) via the task-based framework.
- **For Paper 2**: heterogeneous treatment effects don't happen uniformly. Firm-level task reassignment plays out differently for workers in different local labour markets.

→ Anchor: extends **Autor (2015)**

nodes.title: P·Acemoglu–Restrepo (2018) — Race Between Man & Machine
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Acemoglu, D. & Restrepo, P. (2018). The race between man and machine: Implications of technology for growth, factor shares, and employment. *American Economic Review*, 108(6), 1488–1542.

---

## Intro

**Modern general-equilibrium model of automation** with endogenous creation of new tasks. Introduces the crucial distinction between:
- **Displacement effect** — automation removes tasks from labour.
- **Reinstatement effect** — new tasks emerge, some assigned to labour.

## Setup

- Continuum of tasks; automation moves cutoff, capital takes over tasks below.
- Endogenous R&D creates new tasks at the frontier, initially assigned to labour.
- Labour share depends on the RACE between displacement and reinstatement.

## Result

- **When reinstatement > displacement**: labour share stable, wages rise.
- **When displacement > reinstatement**: labour share falls, wages stagnate.
- 1987–2017 US: displacement > reinstatement → falling labour share.

## Contribution

- Formalises the "task destruction vs creation" narrative.
- Explains observed decline in US labour share via task-based mechanism.
- **For Paper 2**: gen-AI dramatically speeds up displacement. Does it also speed up reinstatement? If yes, labour share protected. If no, sharp reallocation losses.

→ Anchor: **Task-based cluster**; child: **A&R (2022)**

nodes.title: P·Acemoglu–Restrepo (2022) — Tasks, Automation & Wage Inequality
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Acemoglu, D. & Restrepo, P. (2022). Tasks, automation, and the rise in U.S. wage inequality. *Econometrica*, 90(5), 1973–2016.

---

## Intro

**Task-based decomposition** of US wage inequality 1980–2016. Answers: how much of the observed inequality rise is attributable to task reallocation between labour and capital?

## Method

- Estimate a full task-based general-equilibrium model.
- Identify parameters from industry × occupation task-share evolution.
- Counterfactuals: what if automation had been slower?

## Findings

- **50–70% of the observed rise in college-wage-premium is due to task automation** (specifically: automation displaced routine-task workers, mostly non-college).
- Automation reallocated tasks from mid-skill to high-skill labour and to capital.
- Modest effect from skill-biased technical change; task-based effects dominate.

## Contribution

- **Most rigorous empirical decomposition** of task-based effects on inequality.
- Quantifies the mechanism ALM (2003), Acemoglu-Autor (2011), A&R (2018) posited.
- **For Paper 2**: if gen-AI shifts task boundaries again, the same mechanism predicts substantial wage-distribution effects. The 50–70% share of past inequality attributable to task reallocation suggests future effects will also be large.

→ Anchor: extends **A&R (2018)**

nodes.title: P·Brynjolfsson–Li–Raymond (2023) — Generative AI at Work
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Brynjolfsson, E., Li, D. & Raymond, L. (2023). Generative AI at work. NBER Working Paper 31161. (Later *QJE* 140(2), 889–942, 2025.)

---

## Intro

**Canonical field study of gen-AI at work.** Uses proprietary data from a Fortune-500 software firm that rolled out a generative-AI conversation assistant to customer-service agents.

## Design

- ~5,179 customer-service agents.
- Staggered rollout of GPT-based assistant across offices.
- Rich individual-level productivity data: issues resolved per hour, resolution time, customer satisfaction.

## Findings

- **Average productivity gain: +14% issues resolved per hour.**
- **Bottom-quartile workers gained +34%** — enormous.
- **Top-quartile workers gained ~0%** — no improvement.
- **Customer satisfaction improved**, particularly for interactions handled by low-tenure agents.
- Effects strongest for the tacit-knowledge dimensions of the job.

## Interpretation

Gen-AI diffuses tacit knowledge from top performers to bottom performers via its training data. **Compresses within-firm productivity distribution.**

## Contribution

- Field-defining benchmark for gen-AI productivity effects.
- **Direct evidence AGAINST skill-biased tech change** in customer service: AI COMPLEMENTS low-skill workers most.
- **For Paper 2**: exactly the winners/losers question. Answer for customer service: low-skill workers WIN.

→ Anchor: **Gen-AI empirical cluster**; child: **Peng et al. (2023) Copilot**

nodes.title: P·Peng et al. (2023) — GitHub Copilot RCT
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Peng, S., Kalliamvakou, E., Cihon, P. & Demirer, M. (2023). The impact of AI on developer productivity: Evidence from GitHub Copilot. arXiv:2302.06590.

---

## Intro

**Randomized controlled trial** of GitHub Copilot (AI code-completion tool based on GPT). First large-scale RCT of gen-AI in software development.

## Design

- 95 developers recruited.
- Randomly assigned to Copilot vs no-Copilot.
- Task: implement an HTTP server in JavaScript.
- Measurement: time to completion, code quality.

## Findings

- **Copilot users completed the task 55.8% faster** (median).
- Effect concentrated among:
  - **Junior developers** (larger relative gain).
  - **Older developers** (larger relative gain — Copilot substitutes for outdated syntax knowledge).
  - Developers less familiar with the language.
- Code quality unchanged or slightly improved.

## Contribution

- Complements BLR (2023) with clean RCT design.
- **Confirms compression pattern**: AI helps those with lower baseline productivity more.
- Central to the debate on gen-AI in high-skill work.
- **For Paper 2**: gen-AI as task-reallocation tool. Junior developers now do senior-developer tasks with Copilot assistance.

→ Anchor: extends **BLR (2023)**

nodes.title: P·Noy–Zhang (2023) — GPT for Professional Writing
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Noy, S. & Zhang, W. (2023). Experimental evidence on the productivity effects of generative artificial intelligence. *Science*, 381(6654), 187–192.

---

## Intro

**Randomized controlled trial** of ChatGPT for mid-level professional writing tasks (marketing copy, HR communication, business analysis). Published in *Science* — indicates the level of interest.

## Design

- 453 college-educated professionals.
- Randomly assigned to ChatGPT vs no-ChatGPT.
- Task: write a short professional document.
- Blind evaluators graded output quality.

## Findings

- **Time to complete task fell 40%** (median).
- **Output quality rose 18%** (blind grader ratings).
- **Between-writer inequality FELL**: low-baseline writers gained most in quality; high-baseline writers gained most in time.
- Time allocation shifted: less time drafting, more time editing.

## Contribution

- Second-major RCT of gen-AI (after Peng et al.); different domain.
- **Confirms compression pattern** across a broader class of knowledge work.
- Task-level substitution: drafting → editing.
- **For Paper 2**: within-task reallocation. AI takes the drafting sub-task; humans keep the editing sub-task. Comparative advantage rearranged.

→ Anchor: **Gen-AI empirical cluster**; child: **Dell'Acqua et al. (2023)**

nodes.title: P·Dell'Acqua et al. (2023) — Jagged Technological Frontier
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Dell'Acqua, F., McFowland III, E., Mollick, E., Lifshitz-Assaf, H., Kellogg, K., Rajendran, S., Krayer, L., Candelon, F. & Lakhani, K. (2023). Navigating the jagged technological frontier: Field experimental evidence of the effects of AI on knowledge worker productivity and quality. Harvard Business School Working Paper 24-013.

---

## Intro

**Large field experiment with Boston Consulting Group** using GPT-4. Tests gen-AI on real consulting tasks with 758 BCG consultants.

## Design

- 18 consulting-realistic tasks.
- Consultants randomly assigned to: no-AI, AI-only, AI + prompt training.
- Tasks fell into two groups (unknown to participants):
  - "Inside the frontier": tasks GPT-4 can do well (creative product ideation, structured analysis).
  - "Outside the frontier": tasks requiring information beyond GPT-4's knowledge or nuanced judgement.

## Findings

- **Inside the frontier**: AI users completed 12.2% more tasks, 25.1% faster, with 40% higher quality.
- **Outside the frontier**: AI users were **19 percentage points more likely to produce INCORRECT answers.** AI misled them.
- **Skill compression**: within tasks inside the frontier, low performers gained more.

## The "jagged frontier"

AI capabilities are non-monotonic: it can do genuinely hard things but fail at things that seem easy. Workers cannot easily predict where the frontier is. **Skill is required to filter AI output.**

## Contribution

- **Central caveat** to the productivity-gain literature: AI can HURT productivity when misapplied.
- Introduces the "jagged frontier" concept, now widely cited.
- **For Paper 2**: task reassignment must respect the frontier. Some tasks should go to AI+human; some should stay human-only; some should NOT use AI at all.

→ Anchor: extends **Noy-Zhang (2023)**

nodes.title: P·Athey–Bryan–Gans (2020) — Human vs AI Decision Authority
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Athey, S., Bryan, K. & Gans, J. S. (2020). The allocation of decision authority to human and artificial intelligence. *AEA Papers and Proceedings*, 110, 80–84.

---

## Intro

**Theoretical framework** for allocating decision authority between humans and AI. Answers: given an AI that can make some decisions, when should the firm delegate, consult, or overrule?

## Setup

- Task with probability $p$ of being "AI-solvable" (AI's accuracy exceeds human's).
- Human decision authority has cost $c_H$; AI has cost $c_A < c_H$.
- Firm's optimal delegation policy depends on: prior belief about $p$, cost gap, and cost of learning $p$.

## Key results

- **Delegate to AI** when confidence in AI capability is high.
- **Consult** (AI recommends, human decides) when confidence is intermediate — expensive but resolves uncertainty.
- **Overrule** (human decides alone) when confidence in AI is low.
- **Learning dynamics**: firm learns $p$ through experience; delegation policy evolves.

## Contribution

- **First formal model** of decision-authority allocation in the AI era.
- Provides the theoretical scaffolding all empirical gen-AI papers implicitly cite.
- **For Paper 2**: exactly the assignment problem, but between HUMANS and AI rather than between two humans. The task reassignment mechanism.

→ Anchor: **Gen-AI empirical cluster**; child: **Beane (2019)**

nodes.title: P·Beane (2019) — Shadow Learning in Robotic Surgery
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Beane, M. (2019). Shadow learning: Building robotic surgical skill when approved means fail. *Administrative Science Quarterly*, 64(1), 87–123.

---

## Intro

**Ethnographic study** of how robotic-surgery adoption disrupts surgical apprenticeship. Two years of field observation across 5 hospitals.

## The problem

Traditional surgical training: senior surgeon operates while junior watches; junior gradually takes over sub-tasks. Robotic surgery: senior surgeon sits at console. Junior cannot physically take over sub-tasks. **Apprenticeship channel breaks.**

## Response — shadow learning

Junior residents secretly:
- Practice on cadavers after hours.
- Watch YouTube videos of robotic surgeries.
- Ask retired non-robotic surgeons for advice.
- Volunteer for the few robotic-free hospitals to gain hands-on experience.

Institutions officially DO NOT support this. Formal training channels have collapsed.

## Contribution

- **Central cautionary tale**: automation of skilled work can foreclose the human learning path.
- Related to broader "hollowing out" of mid-skill jobs — automation removes the training rungs of career ladders.
- **For Paper 2**: if gen-AI takes over the "junior-level" cognitive tasks (drafting, coding boilerplate, summarizing), how do juniors gain the tacit expertise they'll need as seniors? This is the DARKEST winners/losers question.
- Long-term implication: today's productivity gains may compromise tomorrow's talent pipeline.

→ Anchor: extends **Athey-Bryan-Gans (2020)**

nodes.title: ▼ REORGANIZATION VALUE · empirical estimates
nodes.content:
# REORGANIZATION VALUE · empirical estimates

**How much productivity does reorganizing work actually generate?**

This is the empirical core of Paper 2. Estimates come from three domains, each with different identification strategies and different magnitudes:

## The three empirical lineages below

**HRM bundle studies** (Ichniowski-Shaw-Prennushi 1997) — clean plant-level identification of coordinated changes in task assignment + teams + incentives. **~7% productivity gain** from complete HRM bundles. Small but very cleanly identified.

**IT + workplace reorganization complementarity** (Bresnahan-Brynjolfsson-Hitt 2002 → Bartel-Ichniowski-Shaw 2007) — firms that combine IT adoption with organizational restructuring gain **more than the sum of the two parts** (super-modularity). Reorganization alone or IT alone under-shoot the joint effect. Direct analog to Paper 2's mechanism, but with IT instead of AI as the enabling technology. **BIS 2007** documents **15–20% gains** in valve manufacturing.

**Management-practice RCTs and macro upper bounds** (Bloom-Eifert-Mahajan-McKenzie-Roberts 2013 → Hsieh-Klenow 2009) — RCT of consulting-driven management-practice reorganization in Indian textile plants shows **~17% productivity gain in year 1**. Hsieh-Klenow's cross-country misallocation study provides the **theoretical upper bound**: eliminating within-industry misallocation would raise TFP by **30–60% in developing countries** vs the US frontier.

## What these estimates tell us about Paper 2's magnitude

- **Lower bound (HRM alone, ISP 1997)**: ~7%
- **Middle range (IT-enabled reorganization, BBH 2002 / BIS 2007)**: 15–20%
- **Consulting-driven reorganization (BEMMR 2013)**: 17%
- **Upper bound from macro misallocation (HK 2009)**: 30–60%
- **Gen-AI single-domain (BLR 2023)**: 14% in customer service

Paper 2's likely magnitude range: **10–30%** for a general firm-level intervention.

## What the literature is missing (Paper 2's opening)

**No published paper cleanly isolates task reassignment as a lever independent of the technology that triggered it.** Reorganization is always observed alongside IT adoption (BBH, BIS), consulting intervention (BEMMR), or AI rollout (BLR). The counterfactual "same technology + no reassignment" is rarely constructed.

Paper 2's contribution: a design that isolates the reassignment margin. The ABM lets you toggle it on/off with fixed AI capability.

→ Anchor: **Reorganization Theory — Core**

nodes.title: P·Ichniowski–Shaw–Prennushi (1997) — HRM Bundles in Steel Lines
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Ichniowski, C., Shaw, K. & Prennushi, G. (1997). The effects of human resource management practices on productivity: A study of steel finishing lines. *American Economic Review*, 87(3), 291–313.

---

## Intro

**Cleanly-identified plant-level study** of how coordinated HRM changes (task assignment + team structure + incentive alignment) affect productivity. Uses a rare setting: 36 steel finishing lines with detailed matched data on organizational practices and output.

## Design

- Panel data on 36 steel finishing lines, monthly frequency.
- Rich measurement of HRM practices: incentive pay, teamwork, flexible job assignment, employment security, extensive training, information sharing.
- **Bundles hypothesis**: HRM practices are complements — changing one alone has little effect; changing them together has large effect.

## Findings

- **Complete HRM bundle → ~7% productivity gain** vs traditional practice.
- **Piecemeal adoption → near-zero gain.** Confirms the complementarity/bundles hypothesis.
- Practices that matter most: performance pay + teamwork + flexible job assignment (the reassignment margin).

## Contribution

- **Foundation for the "bundles" literature** in HRM economics.
- Cleanly identified via within-plant variation over time.
- **For Paper 2**: shows that task reassignment ALONE doesn't work — must be bundled with other changes. Suggests Paper 2's ABM should model reassignment × contract × team-structure jointly.

→ Anchor: **Reorganization value cluster**

nodes.title: P·Bresnahan–Brynjolfsson–Hitt (2002) — IT + Reorganization Complementarity
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Bresnahan, T. F., Brynjolfsson, E. & Hitt, L. M. (2002). Information technology, workplace organization, and the demand for skilled labor: Firm-level evidence. *Quarterly Journal of Economics*, 117(1), 339–376.

---

## Intro

**Seminal empirical study of IT–organization complementarity.** Answers: do firms that combine IT adoption with organizational restructuring get more than the sum of the two parts?

## Design

- Firm-level panel data: ~400 large US firms, 1987–1994.
- Measures: IT capital stock, use of decentralized decision-making, teamwork, skill composition.
- Test: is the interaction term IT × reorganization significantly positive?

## Findings

- **YES — strong super-modularity between IT and reorganization.**
- Firms adopting IT + reorganizing had productivity gains that exceeded the sum of IT-alone gain plus reorganization-alone gain.
- The complementarity was concentrated in the demand for skilled labor (decision-authority reorganization increased returns to cognitive skill).

## Contribution

- **Foundation for the "IT–organization complementarity" literature.**
- Directly relevant to Paper 2: gen-AI is the modern analog to 1990s IT; the same complementarity mechanism predicts firms that reorganize alongside AI adoption will gain more than the sum of the parts.
- Motivates the ABM design where AI capability and reassignment are separate levers whose interaction matters.

→ Anchor: **Reorganization value cluster**; child: **BIS 2007**

nodes.title: P·Bartel–Ichniowski–Shaw (2007) — IT + Process Re-engineering
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Bartel, A., Ichniowski, C. & Shaw, K. (2007). How does information technology affect productivity? Plant-level comparisons of product innovation, process improvement, and worker skills. *Quarterly Journal of Economics*, 122(4), 1721–1758.

---

## Intro

Extends BBH 2002 with **plant-level micro-data on valve manufacturers.** Provides one of the cleanest identifications of the IT + reorganization mechanism.

## Design

- 212 valve-manufacturing plants, panel 1997–2005.
- Detailed measurement of IT adoption (CAD/CAM, ERP), process re-engineering, and worker-skill composition.
- Instrumental-variable identification using pre-existing IT investments as an instrument.

## Findings

- **Plants adopting IT + process re-engineering saw 15–20% productivity gains** relative to plants adopting IT alone.
- **Product innovation** was the primary channel: IT enabled reorganized production, which enabled new product introductions.
- Worker-skill composition shifted toward higher cognitive skill demand (echoing BBH 2002).

## Contribution

- Cleanest micro-identification of the IT-reorganization complementarity.
- **For Paper 2**: 15–20% is a middle-of-range estimate. Suggests Paper 2's target magnitude for AI-enabled reorganization is realistic.
- Confirms BBH 2002 at the plant level with cleaner identification.

→ Anchor: extends **BBH 2002**

nodes.title: P·Bloom–Eifert–Mahajan–McKenzie–Roberts (2013) — India Management RCT
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Bloom, N., Eifert, B., Mahajan, A., McKenzie, D. & Roberts, J. (2013). Does management matter? Evidence from India. *Quarterly Journal of Economics*, 128(1), 1–51.

---

## Intro

**The cleanest RCT of management-practice reorganization ever run.** Answers: does professional management (task allocation + monitoring + quality control) actually cause productivity gains, or is the correlation confounded?

## Design

- 20 Indian textile plants near Mumbai randomly assigned to receive intensive consulting (Accenture) or none.
- Consulting focused on 38 management practices covering: factory operations, quality control, inventory management, HRM.
- Baseline + 1-year outcomes on productivity, quality, output.

## Findings

- **~17% productivity gain in year 1** for treated plants vs controls.
- Gains persisted after consultants left (partial retention).
- Effects concentrated in factory-floor task reorganization: better job assignment, cleaner workflows, quality control at each station.
- Management-practice gains alone explain **~35% of the productivity gap** between India and US textile production.

## Contribution

- **Gold-standard causal evidence** that management practices (including task reorganization) cause productivity.
- **For Paper 2**: 17% is a strong reference number. RCT design means it's clean of confounding. Sets the "reasonable magnitude" bar for reorganization interventions.
- Motivated a large follow-up literature on management-consulting experiments.

→ Anchor: **Reorganization value cluster**; child: **Hsieh-Klenow 2009**

nodes.title: P·Hsieh–Klenow (2009) — Misallocation and TFP
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Hsieh, C.-T. & Klenow, P. J. (2009). Misallocation and manufacturing TFP in China and India. *Quarterly Journal of Economics*, 124(4), 1403–1448.

---

## Intro

**Field-defining macro paper on misallocation.** Uses a monopolistic-competition model to estimate the aggregate TFP loss from misallocation of capital and labor across manufacturing plants within the same industry.

## Method

- Model: heterogeneous plants within each 4-digit industry, monopolistic competition, Cobb-Douglas production.
- Under efficient allocation, marginal revenue products would be equalized across plants.
- Observed dispersion of revenue products → measure of misallocation.
- Counterfactual: what TFP would we observe if misallocation were eliminated (to US level)?

## Findings

- **China 1998**: eliminating misallocation would raise manufacturing TFP by **30–50%**.
- **India 1994**: **40–60%** TFP gain.
- Sources of misallocation: distortionary taxes, credit constraints, size-dependent regulations, labour market frictions.
- Even the US has misallocation; benchmark is "as good as US" not "first-best".

## Contribution

- **Establishes the upper-bound estimate** for how much productivity is lost to misallocation across the economy.
- Massive follow-up literature: Restuccia-Rogerson 2008 (methodology), Bils-Klenow-Ruane 2020 (updated estimates), Adamopoulos-Restuccia 2014 (agriculture).
- **For Paper 2**: the upper-bound reference. If a single firm's task reassignment can capture even a fraction of the within-industry misallocation, gains could be very large. Says the "ceiling" of the reorganization value is HIGH.

→ Anchor: extends **BEMMR 2013**

nodes.title: ▼ Skill Heterogeneity & Mismatch Value · [PAPER 2 CORE]
nodes.content:
# Skill Heterogeneity & Mismatch Value · [PAPER 2 CORE]

**The modern empirical literature quantifying value lost to worker-task mismatch.** This is the PRIMARY cluster for Paper 2 — every paper below directly measures the counterpart to $V^{*}$.

## What these papers measure

Given matched employer-employee data with multi-dimensional skill measures ($\alpha_i \in \mathbb{R}^K$ per worker, $\sigma_j \in \mathbb{R}^K$ per job requirements), estimate:

$$\text{Mismatch}_i \;=\; d(\alpha_i, \sigma_{j(i)}) \;\;\; \text{vs.} \;\;\; \text{Mismatch}^{*}_i = \min_j d(\alpha_i, \sigma_j)$$

and the productivity gap between observed and best-matched.

## Three empirical lineages

**Individual-level task heterogeneity within occupations** (Autor-Handel 2013 → Yamaguchi 2012)
- Occupation FE alone miss substantial within-occupation heterogeneity.
- Individual task profiles predict wages beyond occupation × industry FE.
- Yamaguchi's structural model estimates lifecycle skill accumulation via task-based human capital.

**Multi-dim skill mismatch quantification** (Lise-Postel-Vinay 2020 → Guvenen-Kuruscu-Tanaka-Wiczer 2020)
- LPV: multi-dim skills + on-the-job search. Sorting explains ~30% of wage variance.
- **GKTW: THE central paper.** Multi-dim skill mismatch causes substantial productivity loss; mismatch decays with tenure but incompletely. Direct empirical estimate of $V^{*}$.

**Match quality + mobility patterns** (Fredriksson-Hensvik-Skans 2018 → Groes-Kircher-Manovskii 2015)
- FHS: Swedish employer-employee data. Better matches → higher entry wages, lower mobility. Documents match value directly.
- GKM: U-shape of occupational mobility by wage — both low- and high-earners switch more, consistent with mismatch-detection models.

## The Paper 2 target magnitude

From these papers, the value of resolving worker-task mismatch is in the **5–20%** productivity range for a typical firm — with substantial heterogeneity across workers, occupations, and mismatch severity. Guvenen et al 2020 give the cleanest structural estimate.

**Note**: this literature measures mismatch under status-quo (limited type observability). Paper 2 asks what would happen if the firm could observe types PERFECTLY — Paper 2's $V^{*}$ is an upper bound to observed-mismatch estimates.

→ Anchor: **Reorganization Theory — Core** — the primary empirical cluster

nodes.title: P·Roy (1951) — Distribution of Earnings
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Roy, A. D. (1951). Some thoughts on the distribution of earnings. *Oxford Economic Papers*, 3(2), 135–146.

---

## Intro

**Founding paper of self-selection models.** In 12 pages, Roy establishes the theoretical framework for what would become one of the most important tools in labour economics. Motivated by the observed shape of earnings distributions (log-normal with fat right tail), Roy asks: given workers with heterogeneous abilities across occupations, and given they self-select, what does the resulting earnings distribution look like?

## Setup

- Two occupations (hunting, fishing).
- Each worker $i$ has ability $(\alpha_{i,H}, \alpha_{i,F})$ drawn from a joint distribution.
- Worker chooses the occupation with the higher expected income.

## The Roy prediction

Aggregate output is **strictly higher** than under random assignment whenever $\text{Corr}(\alpha_H, \alpha_F) < 1$. The value gain from self-selection depends on:
- **Variance** of each dimension (more heterogeneity → more sorting value).
- **Correlation** across dimensions (lower correlation → more comparative advantage → more sorting value).

## Contribution

- **Template for all subsequent assignment models** (Sattinger 1993, Costinot-Vogel 2010, Guvenen et al 2020, etc.).
- Explains the observed log-normal earnings distribution as a consequence of self-selection, not just underlying ability distribution.
- **For Paper 2**: the ORIGINAL statement of "value from sorting". Every empirical mismatch paper below traces back to Roy's insight. $V^{*}$ is Roy's aggregate output gain generalized to $N$ workers × $K$ tasks.

→ Anchor: **Roy & Assignment theory cluster**

nodes.title: P·Heckman–Sedlacek (1985) — Empirical Roy Model
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Heckman, J. J. & Sedlacek, G. (1985). Heterogeneity, aggregation, and market wage functions: An empirical model of self-selection in the labor market. *Journal of Political Economy*, 93(6), 1077–1125.

---

## Intro

**First rigorous structural estimation of the Roy model.** Answers: can we empirically identify the underlying joint distribution of skills across occupations from observed self-selection outcomes?

## Setup

- Two-sector Roy model (union vs non-union manufacturing).
- Wages depend on skill × sector.
- Workers self-select into sectors based on comparative advantage.
- Estimation from CPS + other US micro data.

## Key results

- Structural estimation recovers the joint skill distribution using self-selection corrections.
- Wage differentials across sectors are ~50% due to composition (sorting) and ~50% due to true wage premium.
- The apparent "union wage premium" overstates the causal effect by a factor of 2 due to self-selection.

## Contribution

- **Founding paper of the empirical Roy literature.** Every subsequent structural sorting paper builds on this framework.
- Introduces the Heckman-selection correction into occupation choice.
