- **For Paper 2**: shows HOW MUCH of observed cross-sector wage differences reflect SORTING vs true wage differences. Direct answer to a Paper 2 sub-question — mismatch reduction ≈ SORTING GAIN component.

→ Anchor: extends **Roy (1951)**

nodes.title: P·Heckman–Honoré (1990) — Empirical Content of Roy Model
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Heckman, J. J. & Honoré, B. E. (1990). The empirical content of the Roy model. *Econometrica*, 58(5), 1121–1149.

---

## Intro

**Non-parametric identification theorem for the Roy model.** Answers: without functional-form assumptions, what CAN and CANNOT be identified from observational data about the underlying skill distribution?

## Result

- Given standard cross-section data (observed wages + observed occupation choice), the **joint distribution of skills is NOT non-parametrically identified** without further assumptions.
- Specifically: without exclusion restrictions or panel data, one cannot separately identify (i) the skill distribution and (ii) the mapping from skill to wage.
- **Rank invariance** or **panel variation** are the two main routes to identification.

## Contribution

- Sets the identification benchmark for all subsequent empirical Roy work.
- Explains why later papers (Lise-Postel-Vinay 2020, Guvenen et al 2020) require rich panel data or specific structural assumptions.
- **For Paper 2**: important caveat — observational estimates of $V^{*}$ have identification limits. The ABM's ability to KNOW true types is what lets Paper 2 sidestep these identification issues.

→ Anchor: extends **Heckman-Sedlacek (1985)**

nodes.title: P·Borjas (1987) — Self-Selection & Immigrant Earnings
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Borjas, G. J. (1987). Self-selection and the earnings of immigrants. *American Economic Review*, 77(4), 531–553.

---

## Intro

**Roy model applied to migration.** Explains observed patterns in immigrant quality (average skill of migrants from country $c$ to US) as the result of self-selection based on returns to skill in origin vs destination.

## Roy application

- Country of origin $c$ has skill distribution $F_c$ + skill return $r_c$.
- Destination (US) has return $r_{\text{US}}$.
- Workers migrate iff net gain (destination wage − origin wage − migration cost) > 0.
- **Positive selection** if $r_{\text{US}} > r_c$: high-skill emigrate (US attracts talent from egalitarian countries).
- **Negative selection** if $r_{\text{US}} < r_c$: low-skill emigrate (US attracts unskilled from unequal countries).

## Empirical findings

- Consistent with the Roy prediction: immigrants from egalitarian countries (Nordic) are positively selected; from unequal countries (Latin America) more mixed.
- Contradicts naive "human-capital" model that predicts uniform positive selection.

## Contribution

- **Canonical empirical application of the Roy model** outside labour-market sector choice.
- Field-defining for the migration-selection literature.
- **For Paper 2**: showcases the general applicability of Roy sorting → task/context selection generates aggregate value through comparative advantage.

→ Anchor: extends **Roy (1951)** — migration application

nodes.title: P·Autor–Handel (2013) — Tasks, Human Capital & Wages
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Autor, D. H. & Handel, M. J. (2013). Putting tasks to the test: Human capital, job tasks, and wages. *Journal of Labor Economics*, 31(S1), S59–S96.

---

## Intro

**Empirical documentation of individual-level task heterogeneity WITHIN occupations.** Shows that occupation-level task measures (as in ALM 2003) miss substantial variation across workers within the same occupation code — meaning worker × task heterogeneity is real and quantifiable.

## Design

- Uses the Princeton Data Improvement Initiative (PDII) survey — direct individual-level measures of tasks performed on the job.
- Merges with earnings data.
- Tests whether individual task profiles predict wages BEYOND occupation × education × experience fixed effects.

## Findings

- **Individual task performance predicts wages significantly beyond occupation FE.** Adds ~20% to R² of wage regression.
- Task heterogeneity within occupations is comparable in magnitude to between-occupation heterogeneity.
- Analytical, managerial, and interactive tasks each have distinct wage returns.

## Contribution

- **First direct empirical evidence** that individual worker task profiles matter for productivity/wages independently of occupation.
- Validates the "multi-dim skill" empirical program (Yamaguchi 2012, Lise-Postel-Vinay 2020, Guvenen et al 2020).
- **For Paper 2**: shows $\{\alpha_{ij}\}$ heterogeneity is measurable and consequential. Justifies the Paper 2 setup where reassignment matters at the INDIVIDUAL level, not just at the occupation level.

→ Anchor: **Skill heterogeneity & mismatch cluster**

nodes.title: P·Yamaguchi (2012) — Tasks & Heterogeneous Human Capital
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Yamaguchi, S. (2012). Tasks and heterogeneous human capital. *Journal of Labor Economics*, 30(1), 1–53.

---

## Intro

**Structural lifecycle model of task-based human capital.** Workers have multi-dimensional skills; jobs use different task bundles; workers accumulate skill in tasks they perform. Estimates the model on NLSY79.

## Setup

- Worker skill: 2-dim (cognitive + motor).
- Jobs are task bundles (cognitive intensity + motor intensity) — from ALM 2003 measures.
- Wage = skill × task-intensity, plus experience premium.
- On-the-job skill accumulation depends on TASKS PERFORMED, not just years worked.

## Findings

- Cognitive skill accumulates faster in cognitive-intensive jobs; motor in motor-intensive jobs.
- Skill accumulation ~30% of lifecycle wage growth (rest from job matching + human capital).
- **Job-switching to better-matched tasks explains significant wage growth**, particularly in early career.

## Contribution

- **First fully-structural estimation** of multi-dim task-based human capital accumulation.
- Establishes that skill × task matching evolves over the lifecycle — an endogenous version of the $\{\alpha_{ij}\}$ matrix.
- **For Paper 2**: shows the α matrix is DYNAMIC. Reassignment doesn't just harvest current comparative advantage — it also shapes future skill accumulation. Suggests Paper 2's ABM should include a dynamic skill-accumulation module.

→ Anchor: extends **Autor-Handel (2013)**

nodes.title: P·Lise–Postel-Vinay (2020) — Multidim Skills, Sorting, Accumulation
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Lise, J. & Postel-Vinay, F. (2020). Multidimensional skills, sorting, and human capital accumulation. *American Economic Review*, 110(8), 2328–2376.

---

## Intro

**Frontier structural paper** on multi-dim skill sorting + on-the-job search + human capital accumulation. Merges the Roy-model sorting with the Postel-Vinay-Robin search framework.

## Setup

- Worker skill: 3-dim (cognitive, manual, interpersonal).
- Jobs require multi-dim skills; wages depend on skill-job match.
- On-the-job search: workers occasionally receive outside offers → move to better matches.
- Skills accumulate in relevant dimensions on the job.

## Findings

- **Sorting explains ~30% of cross-worker wage variance.**
- Skill accumulation ~20%; search frictions + luck ~50%.
- **Multi-dim skills essential**: 1-dim models miss 40% of sorting effects.
- Better matches on cognitive skill are worth more than better matches on manual skill (higher wage return per unit of match quality).

## Contribution

- **Cleanest structural estimate** of the value of skill-job sorting.
- Provides the mid-range benchmark: pure sorting (no productivity gain from reassignment, just re-matching) generates ~30% of wage variance.
- **For Paper 2**: direct empirical anchor. If reassignment resolves even half the observed sorting variance, $V^{*}$ is on the order of ~15% of the wage bill.

→ Anchor: extends **Yamaguchi (2012)**

nodes.title: P·Guvenen–Kuruscu–Tanaka–Wiczer (2020) — Multidim Skill Mismatch
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Guvenen, F., Kuruscu, B., Tanaka, S. & Wiczer, D. (2020). Multidimensional skill mismatch. *American Economic Journal: Macroeconomics*, 12(1), 210–244.

---

## Intro

**THE central paper for Paper 2.** Directly measures the productivity loss from multi-dim worker-task mismatch and estimates how much of it is resolved by job mobility over the lifecycle.

## Setup

- Worker skill vector $\alpha_i \in \mathbb{R}^3$ (verbal, math, spatial from ASVAB).
- Job requirement vector $\sigma_j \in \mathbb{R}^3$ (from O*NET).
- **Mismatch**: distance $d(\alpha_i, \sigma_{j(i)})$.
- Wage regression: $\log w = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \alpha + \beta_2 \sigma + \beta_3 \text{mismatch}$.

## Findings

- **Mismatch has large negative wage effect**: 1 SD of mismatch → ~10% wage penalty.
- Mismatch decays with tenure: workers gradually find better matches.
- **BUT mismatch never fully resolves**: even at 30 years of experience, substantial mismatch remains.
- Aggregate mismatch resolution contributes ~15–20% to lifecycle wage growth.

## Contribution

- **Most direct empirical answer to Paper 2's core question.** Quantifies value lost to mismatch as ~10% per SD.
- Shows resolution is incomplete → substantial reassignment gain remains available even in mature workers.
- **For Paper 2 target**: $V^{*}$ from perfect reassignment (Paper 2 counterfactual) is an upper bound on GKTW's observed mismatch — plausibly 10-20% of wages / output.

→ Anchor: **Skill heterogeneity & mismatch cluster** — the central paper

nodes.title: P·Fredriksson–Hensvik–Skans (2018) — Mismatch & Match Quality
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Fredriksson, P., Hensvik, L. & Skans, O. N. (2018). Mismatch of talent: Evidence on match quality, entry wages, and job mobility. *American Economic Review*, 108(11), 3303–3338.

---

## Intro

**Cleanest empirical mismatch measurement using Swedish employer-employee registry data.** Direct measure of worker skill × job requirement match quality, linked to wage and mobility outcomes.

## Design

- Swedish military enlistment tests (cognitive + non-cognitive skills) for all conscripted males.
- Merged with employer-employee panel data.
- Job requirements from occupational task measures.
- Measure: multi-dim distance between individual skills and job requirements.

## Findings

- **Better matches → 5–10% higher entry wages**, cleanly identified.
- Better matches → **20–30% lower quit probability**.
- Match quality persists: workers who start in good matches STAY in good matches (path dependency).
- **Mismatch decays only slowly**: after 5 years, initial mismatch still explains 40% of current mismatch.

## Contribution

- **Cleanest reduced-form estimate** of mismatch effects.
- Complements GKTW 2020 (structural) with cleaner identification (Swedish register + military tests).
- **For Paper 2**: provides the empirical anchor for entry-wage effects of matching, and quantifies mismatch persistence.

→ Anchor: **Skill heterogeneity & mismatch cluster**

nodes.title: P·Groes–Kircher–Manovskii (2015) — U-Shape of Occupational Mobility
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Groes, F., Kircher, P. & Manovskii, I. (2015). The u-shapes of occupational mobility. *Review of Economic Studies*, 82(2), 659–692.

---

## Intro

**Empirical documentation of U-shape of occupational mobility by wage.** Both low-wage AND high-wage workers within an occupation are more likely to switch occupations than mid-wage workers.

## Empirical fact

- Danish employer-employee registry, 1980-2006.
- Within any occupation, quit-to-different-occupation probability is U-shaped in relative wage.
- **Low earners quit** because they discover they're a bad match.
- **High earners quit** because their skill outstrips the occupation's demand.
- **Mid earners stay** — they've found a decent match.

## Model interpretation

Consistent with a **learning + reassignment** model:
- Workers don't observe their own type perfectly.
- They observe relative wage as signal about match quality.
- Both very-low and very-high wages signal mismatch (in different directions) → prompt occupation change.

## Contribution

- **Documents the empirical footprint of mismatch resolution via mobility.**
- Distinguishes mismatch-detection from human-capital models (latter predicts monotone mobility in wage).
- **For Paper 2**: quantifies how much reassignment happens organically vs how much would require firm intervention. If firms can observe types faster than workers can discover them, firm-driven reassignment beats worker-driven mobility.

→ Anchor: **Skill heterogeneity & mismatch cluster**

nodes.title: ▼ Field experiments
nodes.content:
# Field experiments 







## The three lineages

**1) Within-firm worker-team assortative matching** (Adhvaryu-Bassi-Nyshadham-Tamayo; WP <- Imran Rasul student)
- **Adhvaryu et al.**: quasi-experimental variation in team composition inside a large Indian garment manufacturer (observes existing assignment variation, doesn't experimentally re-assign.). Estimates the productivity gain from optimal assortative matching. They estimate worker productivity (good vs bad worker), managers productivity (good vs bad manager) and the interaction (is there a compelmentarity in matching good workers and good managers) -> they confirm the **positive assortative matching** hypothesis (+ 1 to 4% productivity gain, running a simulation). But find that NAM is used to guarantee minimum standards of production 
- **Chan 2016**: they change "who does what" in an hospital (very silly, introduce patient assignment), positive effects  on waiting times, quality of the service, patient satisfaction

**2) Manager-driven reassignment under different incentives** (Bandiera-Barankay-Rasul 2007 QJE): 
"firm level experiment in which we engineered an exogenous change in managerial compensation from fixed wages to performance pay based on the average productivity of lower-tier workers". Theory assumes managerial effort has a higher return on more able workers. So we should see managers respond to incentives by targeting their efforts towards more able workers, implying that both the mean and the disper-
sion increase. Second, managers select out the least able workers, implying that the mean increases but the dispersion may decrease. Managers target their effort towards high ability workers, and the least able workers are less likely to be selected into employment

Some numbers: 
- Higher productivity: Introducing performance-based pay for managers increased average worker productivity by 21%.
- Greater productivity differences: Productivity became more uneven across workers, with the coefficient of variation increasing by 38%. Managers focused their effort on the most capable workers, who became significantly more productive, while less capable workers saw little or no improvement., 
- Relative contributions: At least half of the 21% productivity gain came from selecting better workers (surprisingly close to Lazear 2000)

**3) Decision-authority reassignment** (Hoffman-Kahn-Li 2018 QJE → Bloom-Liang-Roberts-Ying 2015 QJE)
- **Hoffman et al.**: firms adopting algorithmic hiring recommendations vs continuing manager discretion. When managers override algorithm, hires are 15-20% worse.
- **Bloom et al.**: RCT of WFH at Ctrip (Chinese travel firm). **13% productivity gain** from reassigning work location. Cleanest RCT of work-organization change.

nodes.title: P·Adhvaryu–Bassi–Nyshadham–Tamayo (2024) — No Line Left Behind
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Adhvaryu, A., Bassi, V., Nyshadham, A. & Tamayo, J. (forthcoming). No line left behind: Assortative matching inside the firm. *Review of Economics and Statistics*, DOI: 10.1162/rest_a_01516. (Online October 2024.)

---

## Intro

**The closest published paper to Paper 2's design.** Directly estimates the productivity gain from optimal assortative matching of workers to teams inside a firm. Uses granular data from a large Indian garment manufacturer with detailed worker productivity records and observed line-team composition.

## Setup

- Indian garment factory with ~100 production lines × ~30 workers per line.
- Each worker has an individual-productivity measure (pieces per shift).
- Team output is a nonlinear function of individual productivities within the line.
- Question: how much would firm output rise if workers were REASSIGNED across lines to maximize aggregate output?

## Identification

Uses quasi-experimental variation in team composition driven by absenteeism + hiring flows to identify:
1. The production function $F(\alpha_1, ..., \alpha_N)$ within a team.
2. The counterfactual optimal assignment $\mu^*$.
3. The productivity gap between observed $\mu_0$ and optimal $\mu^*$.

## Findings

- **Optimal assortative matching would raise firm output by 1–5%** relative to current (near-random) assignment.
- Complementarities are moderate — the production function has meaningful positive assortative matching returns.
- Gains concentrated in lines with high skill variance among workers.

## Contribution

- **Cleanest published measure of within-firm assortative-matching value.**
- Direct empirical bridge between assignment theory (Costinot-Vogel 2010) and firm reality.
- **For Paper 2**: THE benchmark paper. Paper 2's $V^*$ target is directly comparable to Adhvaryu et al.'s ~1-5%. Paper 2 goes beyond by (i) considering MULTI-dimensional skills, not just single productivity, (ii) simulating the counterfactual under different AI-observability regimes, (iii) linking to broader task landscape.

→ Anchor: **Field experiments cluster** — the primary reference paper

nodes.title: P·Chan (2016) — Teamwork & Moral Hazard in the ED
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Chan, D. C. (2016). Teamwork and moral hazard: Evidence from the emergency department. *Journal of Political Economy*, 124(3), 734–770.

---

## Intro

**Random-assignment field study** of nurse-team composition effects on ED productivity. Uses shift-scheduling procedures that quasi-randomly assign nurses to teams.

## Setup

- Emergency department: physicians + nurses working in teams.
- Shift scheduling gives quasi-random variation in team composition.
- Outcome: patient throughput, patient outcomes.

## Findings

- **Substantial team-composition effects**: swap-in of a high-productivity nurse raises team output by 5-10% depending on the shift.
- Peer effects (moral hazard channel): high-effort nurses raise the effort of others in the same team.
- Optimal team composition can raise ED productivity by ~10-15% over random assignment.

## Contribution

- **Cleanest identification of team-composition value** in a real workplace via quasi-random assignment.
- Confirms the Roy/assortative-matching prediction: matching matters, and observed matching is far from optimal.
- **For Paper 2**: high-stakes complement to Adhvaryu et al. The ED setting is very different from a garment factory but the underlying result is the same — reassignment generates non-trivial value.

→ Anchor: extends **Adhvaryu et al.** — team-composition experimental evidence

nodes.title: P·Bandiera–Barankay–Rasul (2007) — Manager Incentives & Worker Reassignment
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Bandiera, O., Barankay, I. & Rasul, I. (2007). Incentives for managers and inequality among workers: Evidence from a firm-level experiment. *Quarterly Journal of Economics*, 122(2), 729–773.

---

## Intro

**Field experiment where managers received performance-based bonuses.** The unintended-but-central effect: managers began reassigning workers to teams differently — cherry-picking high-productivity workers into their own teams and reallocating tasks to favor them.

## Setup

- UK soft-fruit farm; same firm as BBR 2005 and BBR 2013 but different experiment.
- Managers (previously flat-paid) randomly assigned to receive performance bonuses based on team output.
- Rich data on worker × field × day productivity + observed manager task-assignment decisions.

## Findings

- **Managers reassigned workers strategically** once given incentives: high-productivity workers pulled onto manager's own team; low-productivity workers relegated.
- **Team productivity rose 21%** on average, but concentrated in already-productive workers.
- **Increased inequality among workers** — low-productivity workers earned LESS after the intervention.

## Contribution

- **Documents reassignment as an endogenous response** to incentive changes.
- Direct empirical evidence that: (i) managers CAN reassign to raise productivity, (ii) reassignment is CONSTRAINED without proper incentives to do so.
- **For Paper 2**: shows the "given contract" framing matters. Manager incentives affect whether reassignment happens. Paper 2's design controls for this by fixing contract while varying reassignment technology.

→ Anchor: **Field experiments cluster**

nodes.title: P·Hoffman–Kahn–Li (2018) — Discretion in Hiring
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Hoffman, M., Kahn, L. B. & Li, D. (2018). Discretion in hiring. *Quarterly Journal of Economics*, 133(2), 765–800.

---

## Intro

**Empirical study of algorithmic hiring vs manager discretion.** Uses data from 15 large firms that adopted a machine-learning-based job-test for entry-level positions. When the algorithm's recommendation and the human hiring manager's judgment disagreed, the human sometimes overrode the algorithm. Hoffman et al. use these override decisions to identify the value of algorithmic vs discretionary hiring.

## Setup

- 15 firms adopting a common ML-based hiring test.
- ~300,000 job applications; ~100,000 hires.
- The firm offers a test designed to predict performance for a particular job in the low- skilled service sector.
- For each candidate: (i) test score (algorithm recommendation), (ii) whether hired, (iii) subsequent tenure/productivity.
- Test scores were shown to managers as a green/yellow/red flag.

## Findings

- testing increases work duration by 26%
- **Managers frequently overrode the algorithm**: 20-40% of hires had lower test scores than rejected candidates.
- **Overrides led to WORSE hires**: 15-20% shorter tenure and lower productivity for algorithm-overridden hires.


## Contribution

- **Cleanest empirical evidence** that algorithmic assignment (of workers to jobs at hiring stage) beats human discretion.
- Direct implication: firm value can be raised by REASSIGNING hiring authority from humans to algorithms.
- **For Paper 2**: reassigning DECISION authority is a form of task reassignment. Provides an upper bound on the value of algorithmic assignment when types are observable via testing.

→ Anchor: **Field experiments cluster**; child: **Bloom et al. (2015) WFH**

nodes.title: P·Bloom–Liang–Roberts–Ying (2015) — Working from Home RCT
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Bloom, N., Liang, J., Roberts, J. & Ying, Z. J. (2015). Does working from home work? Evidence from a Chinese experiment. *Quarterly Journal of Economics*, 130(1), 165–218.

---

## Intro

**Landmark RCT of work-location reassignment.** Chinese travel firm Ctrip randomly assigned call-center employees to work-from-home vs office for 9 months. Measures productivity, promotions, and quit rates.

## Setup

- ~250 volunteers eligible to WFH.
- Randomly assigned: WFH (4 days/week) vs office.
- 9-month experiment.
- Outcomes: calls handled, minutes per call, quit rate, promotion.

## Findings

- **WFH raised productivity by 13%.**
  - +9% from more time worked per shift (fewer breaks, less commuting-based sick leave).
  - +4% from more calls per hour (quieter environment).
- Quit rate fell 50%.
- **BUT**: promotion rate fell HALF as much for WFH workers.
- After the experiment, 50% of WFH workers wanted to return to the office (loneliness, career concerns).

## Contribution

- **First rigorous RCT of remote work.** Foundational for a huge subsequent literature on WFH.
- Documents the productivity vs career-progression tradeoff of location reassignment.
- **For Paper 2**: cleanest example of a work-organization RCT. Directly demonstrates that reassigning workers (across the office/home boundary) produces measurable output effects. Complements Adhvaryu et al. (within-firm reassignment) with a different-dimension reassignment.

→ Anchor: extends **Hoffman-Kahn-Li (2018)** — different type of decision-authority reassignment

nodes.title: Methodologies
nodes.content:
## Approaches (just the ones already realized, not the full set of what i have in mind): 


** 1) Causal Empirics**: self selection is a huge issue... (extra math course offered to a class... who will join..). Very foundamental econometric issue that inhibt any pubblication. 
Sell to clients as three separate mini-products: reorg-only, incentive-only, full-stack. Each arm is a legitimate offering. Famous methodology: to avoid self selection promote some clients to test freely the product. 

| Arm | Reorganisation | Incentive contract |
|---|---|---|
| **B** (0, 0) | Old assignment $\mu_0$ | Flat wage $A_0$ |
| **R** (1, 0) | **Quindi reorganises** to $\mu^*$ | Flat wage $A_0$ |
| **I** (0, 1) | Old assignment $\mu_0$ | **Quindi contract $A_j$** |
| **F** (1, 1) | **Quindi reorganises** + **Quindi contract** | |


## Strategy 2 — Staged rollout (near-best)

If 2×2 is politically hard, run in phases:

- **Phase 1** (months 1–3): random $A_j$ treatment, **assignment frozen** at $\mu_0$ → clean $\hat\tau_{\text{incent}}$.
- **Phase 2** (months 4–6): allow Quindi to reorganise → clean $\hat\tau_{\text{total}}$, then $\hat\tau_{\text{reorg}} = \hat\tau_{\text{total}} - \hat\tau_{\text{incent}}$.

**Assumption**: incentive effect stable across phases + interaction effect unidentifiable (my simulation indicicates this is a severe concern)

---

## Strategy 3 — Within-worker-within-task fixed effects (observational)

Panel data with workers doing multiple tasks over time; some clients adopt one Quindi module before the other (staggered adoption):

$$y_{ikt} \;=\; \alpha_i + \gamma_k + \delta_t + \tau_{\text{incent}} \cdot Q^{\text{incent}}_{it} + \tau_{\text{reorg}} \cdot Q^{\text{reorg}}_{it} + \varepsilon_{ikt}$$

where $y_{ikt}$ is output of worker $i$ on task $k$ at time $t$; $Q^{\text{incent}}_{it}$, $Q^{\text{reorg}}_{it}$ are module-adoption indicators.

- $\tau_{\text{incent}}$ identified from same $(i, k)$ pre vs post contract switch.
- $\tau_{\text{reorg}}$ identified from worker crossing tasks under stable contract.

recall: controls are a whitin group comparison...

---

trash.title: A5. Deferred Compensation / Seniority Pay (Lazear 1979, 1981)
trash.content:
**Signal**: tenure. Pay < marginal product early, > marginal product late.

**Solves**
- Bonds worker to firm — being fired for shirking forfeits back-loaded pay.
- Long horizon dampens the ratchet incentive (F3): giving up short-run output for long-run tenure.
- Long horizon dampens Goodhart bunching (F6): quarter-end games matter less if 30-year payoff dominates.
- Solves moral hazard when short-run output isn't measurable but reputation shapes retention.

**Breaks**
- Requires credible commitment from firm not to fire senior workers arbitrarily.
- Creates incentives for mandatory retirement (Lazear 1979).
- Weakens mobility — inefficient if outside options shift.

**Use when**: firm-specific human capital matters, output hard to measure period-by-period, firm has commitment techno

trash.title: A6. Career Concerns / Implicit Incentives (Fama 1980; Holmström 1982)
trash.content:
**Signal**: your *future outside wage*, priced by the labor market from observed output.

**Solves**
- Market averages many noisy signals over time → attacks measurement noise (F1).
- Naturally captures multidimensional output — market cares about overall ability, not one metric (F2).
- Removes the ratchet (F3): market has no incentive to raise your standard if you produce more.
- Continuous market pricing → no threshold to bunch at (F6).

**Breaks**
- Horizon effect: incentive weakens toward retirement (Gibbons–Murphy 1992).
- Effort tilts to visible, market-legible activities → private-value tasks under-provided.
- Requires market observability of individual output.

**Use when**: high-visibility labor markets (CEOs, academics, professional services).
